items.lessonTitle: everyone on the floor, everyone the same meal

neighbors.heading: the guest as God
neighbors.text: Today the langar fed anyone who walked in, no questions asked. Hindus have an old line for the person at the door: atithi devo bhava, the guest is as God. It comes from the Taittiriya Upanishad, right beside honoring your mother, father and teacher. Many Hindu temples serve free meals to visitors too, a gift called annadanam, the giving of food.
neighbors.difference: In the Hindu ideal, the host honors the guest as divine. In langar there's no host and no guest of honor: everyone, the servers included, sits in the same row on the same floor.
neighbors.shared: a hungry stranger at the door is someone to feed, not question.
neighbors.sources: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11.2 (paraphrase) · annadanam in Hindu temples (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: all who are hungry
neighbors.text: Today the langar fed anyone who walked in: no ticket, no questions. Early in the Passover seder, Jews lift the matzah and say in Aramaic, ha lachma anya: this is the bread of affliction; let all who are hungry come and eat. And Genesis tells of Abraham, sitting at his tent door in the heat of the day, running out to welcome three strangers.
neighbors.difference: The seder's invitation is spoken at a family table each Passover, over a meal that tells Israel's own story of freedom. Langar is a public kitchen, open every day, where the seating itself teaches that everyone is level.
neighbors.shared: the door is open, and the bread is for whoever's hungry.
neighbors.sources: Passover Haggadah, Ha Lachma Anya (paraphrase) · Genesis 18:1-8 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the left hand doesn't know
neighbors.text: Today's seva happened where nobody was watching: shoes lined up, plates scrubbed, no names. Jesus said something close about giving: "But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth: That thine alms may be in secret." Keep it so quiet, the picture suggests, that even you barely notice.
neighbors.difference: Jesus adds that the Father "which seeth in secret" will reward it. Sikh teaching asks for seva with no reward in mind at all; the service itself is the way of drawing near to God.
neighbors.shared: the kindest work often happens where nobody's watching.

neighbors.heading: the hidden gift
neighbors.text: Today's seva happened out of sight: a plate scrubbed by someone who'll never know your name. The Qur'an speaks of giving the same way: "If ye publish your almsgiving, it is well, but if ye hide it and give it to the poor, it will be better for you." A well-known hadith praises one who gives so quietly the left hand doesn't know what the right gave.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, zakat is a set duty, a yearly share of wealth, alongside voluntary charity. Sikhs give dasvandh, a tenth, too; seva itself is mostly given with hands and time: cooking, cleaning, minding shoes.
neighbors.shared: giving in secret keeps the gift about the other person.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 2:271 (Pickthall 1930) · Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith of the seven in God's shade (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: two or three gathered
neighbors.text: Today's word was sangat: you become like the company you keep, and the true congregation is where the one name is spoken. Catholics hold a promise of Jesus close: "For where there are two or three gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." It's one reason Catholics gather each Sunday, not only pray alone.
neighbors.difference: Catholics believe Christ himself is present where they gather, and most fully in the Eucharist at Mass. Sikhs hold that the Guru is present in the sangat, gathered around the Guru Granth Sahib and the Name.
neighbors.shared: nobody is meant to walk the path alone.

neighbors.heading: the whole of the path
neighbors.text: Today's word was sangat, the company that carries you like a current. Buddhists take refuge in three jewels, and the third is the sangha, the community. In one sutta, Ananda suggests that good friendship is half the holy life. The Buddha corrects him: not half. Admirable friendship is the whole of the holy life.
neighbors.difference: In the refuges, sangha often means the community of monks and nuns, or those far along the path. Sangat is any gathering where the Name is sung, open to whoever walks in.
neighbors.shared: good friends aren't extra to the path; they're part of it.
neighbors.sources: Upaddha Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 45.2 (paraphrase) · the Three Refuges (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: of thine own
neighbors.text: Today Nanak kept counting tera, tera: yours, all of it yours. When King David gathered gifts for the Temple, he prayed the same idea: "for all things come of thee, and of thine own have we given thee." A rabbi in the Mishnah says it too: give to God from what is God's, for you and all you have are God's.
neighbors.difference: In Jewish life this idea is shaped into law, with set ways to give, like the tithe and tzedakah. Nanak's tera was a moment, not a rule: the counting simply stopped, and every scoop was yours.
neighbors.shared: what we hold is lent to us, so we hold it open-handed.
neighbors.sources: 1 Chronicles 29:14 (KJV) · Pirkei Avot 3:7 (3:8 in some editions) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: not lost, given back
neighbors.text: Today Nanak looked at the grain, the scale and his own hands, and said: yours. The Stoic teacher Epictetus gave his students a similar habit. Never say of anything, I have lost it; say, I have given it back. Land, a child, a spouse: all on loan. So while you have it, he said, care for it like a traveler at an inn.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus speaks of returning things to the one who gave them, in a Stoic sense of nature and the gods. Tera is spoken to one loving God, as devotion, and it made Nanak more generous, not only calmer.
neighbors.shared: holding things loosely can make a person kinder and freer.

neighbors.heading: evil turned to good
neighbors.text: Today Sajjan heard a song about shiny bronze, recognized himself, and gave back what he'd stolen. The Qur'an leaves that door open too. After naming grave wrongs, it adds: "Save him who repenteth and believeth and doth righteous work; as for such, Allah will change their evil deeds to good deeds." Muslims call that turning tawba.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, tawba is between the person and God directly; no one stands in between. Sajjan's turn came through the Guru's song, and in the Sikh telling the Guru's presence opened the door.
neighbors.shared: no one is past turning around.

neighbors.heading: the robber who became a poet
neighbors.text: Today a friendly innkeeper who robbed his guests heard a hymn and turned. Hindus tell a story like it. Tradition says Valmiki was once a highway robber who stopped the wrong traveler, a holy man, and was set to repeating Rama's name. He sat so long an anthill grew over him, and he rose a sage who would compose the Ramayana.
neighbors.difference: In the Hindu story, the change comes slowly, through years of repeating a divine name. Sajjan's came in one night, and making it right meant giving back what he'd stolen.
neighbors.shared: even the worst chapter doesn't have to be the last.
neighbors.sources: Valmiki tradition, as told in later Ramayana retellings (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the lotus, unsmeared
neighbors.text: Today Nanak told the mountain yogis to live like a lotus: in the water, floating clean. The Buddha reached for the same flower. A lotus is born in the water, he said, grows in the water, rises above it, and stands unsmeared by it. In the same way, he said of himself, born and grown in the world, he lived unsmeared by the world.
neighbors.difference: The Buddha spoke as one who had left home for the homeless life, and many of his followers became monks and nuns. Nanak gave the lotus to householders: stay with your family and your work, and float.
neighbors.shared: you can live in the thick of the world and stay clean.

neighbors.heading: in the world, not of it
neighbors.text: Today Nanak turned down the cabin in the mountains: stay, work, love your people, and float. On the night before he died, Jesus prayed for his friends the same way: "I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil. They are not of the world, even as I am not of the world."
neighbors.difference: For Christians, being "not of the world" means belonging to Christ, kept by the Father. Many Christian traditions also honor monks and nuns who leave ordinary life; Sikh teaching asks every follower to live as a householder.
neighbors.shared: staying in ordinary life can be the holy choice.

neighbors.heading: a sound mind in a sound body
neighbors.text: Today a Guru cheered on wrestlers, because on his path the body isn't the enemy. The Roman poet Juvenal poked fun at what people pray for: money, fame, a long life. If you must ask for something, he wrote, ask for mens sana in corpore sano, a sound mind in a sound body, and a brave heart that doesn't fear death.
neighbors.difference: Juvenal was a satirist, not a teacher of a path, and he leaves the choosing to the gods. At Khadur, strength had a direction: a body fit to serve, with the real wrestling done against ego, greed and anger.
neighbors.shared: taking care of your body is part of taking care of your soul.

neighbors.heading: so run that you may obtain
neighbors.text: Today the ground at Khadur was a real wrestling pit and a picture of the fight inside. Saint Paul used the stadium the same way: "Know you not that they that run in the race, all run indeed, but one receiveth the prize? So run that you may obtain." He even pictured himself as a fighter, "not as one beating the air."
neighbors.difference: For Paul, the prize is an "incorruptible" crown, life with Christ. For Sikhs, the arena is the world itself, and the opponents are inside: ego, greed and anger.
neighbors.shared: the body is part of the path, not in its way.

neighbors.heading: rounds around the center
neighbors.text: Today a Sikh couple walked four rounds around the Guru Granth Sahib, one stanza for each. A Hindu wedding walks circles too. The couple circles the sacred fire, Agni, as their witness, and in the saptapadi they take seven steps together, with a vow at each step. After the seventh, tradition says, they are friends for life.
neighbors.difference: In a Hindu wedding the fire is the witness, and vows are made at each step. In the Anand Karaj, the center is the Guru's word, and the four rounds trace the soul's own path toward God.
neighbors.shared: a marriage is a path you walk, step by step, side by side.
neighbors.sources: Hindu wedding rites: the pheras and the saptapadi (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: seven circles
neighbors.text: Today the lavan walked a couple round and round, with the word at the center. At many Jewish weddings, especially Ashkenazi ones, the bride circles the groom, often seven times, under the chuppah, the wedding canopy. Some link the custom to a line in Jeremiah: "A woman shall compass a man." Then seven blessings are sung over the couple.
neighbors.difference: Under the chuppah, the bride circles the groom, and a marriage contract, the ketubah, is read aloud. In the lavan, the two walk together around the scripture, as a picture of the soul's marriage to God.
neighbors.shared: love gets walked into, one circle at a time.
neighbors.sources: Jeremiah 31:22 (KJV) · Jewish wedding customs: the circling and the sheva brachot (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: pray for them
neighbors.text: Today Guru Arjan's own brother set himself up against him, and the Guru didn't curse him; he kept working and left him to God. Jesus taught: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you." Paul put it in one line: "Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good."
neighbors.difference: Jesus frames it as active love for the enemy, even blessing. Guru Arjan sang that no one is his enemy or a stranger; as Sikhs tell it, he trusted God with the outcome and kept serving.
neighbors.shared: you don't have to become like the one who hurts you.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 5:44 (KJV) · Romans 12:21 (KJV) · Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1299 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: no fear this day
neighbors.text: Today a jealous brother made trouble for years, and Guru Arjan didn't strike back. The Qur'an tells of a prophet with jealous brothers too: Yusuf, thrown into a well, who rises high in Egypt. When his brothers finally stand before him, he says: "Have no fear this day! May Allah forgive you." Another verse: "Repel the evil deed with one which is better."
neighbors.difference: Yusuf's story ends with the family reunited, forgiven face to face. The Sikh telling of Prithi Chand ends without a reunion; Guru Arjan's answer was to leave him to God and keep his own work going.
neighbors.shared: a brother's wrong doesn't have to write your answer.

neighbors.heading: Brother Sun, Sister Water
neighbors.text: Today the boy Har Rai broke a flower with his robe, and learned to walk gently for life. Catholics have a saint who walked that way: Francis of Assisi. In his Canticle of the Creatures he praises God for Brother Sun, Sister Moon, Sister Water and Mother Earth, as if all of creation were family. Stories say he moved worms off the road.
neighbors.difference: Francis praises God for the creatures, as brothers and sisters made by one Creator, never as God. Sikh scripture sees the one light present within all creation, so carelessness toward it is carelessness toward that light.
neighbors.shared: the more room you take up, the more gently you walk.
neighbors.sources: Francis of Assisi, Canticle of the Creatures (paraphrase) · Thomas of Celano, First Life of Saint Francis (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the bee and the flower
neighbors.text: Today a boy learned to carry his robe close, so it wouldn't break the flowers. The Dhammapada gives a picture of the same care: "As the bee collects nectar and departs without injuring the flower, or its colour or scent, so let a sage dwell in his village." Take what you need, and leave the place as lovely as you found it.
neighbors.difference: The bee verse is advice for monks on the alms round, taking only what they need. Har Rai's lesson was for someone with power, a future Guru, learning that a big presence must move with care.
neighbors.shared: gentleness reaches even a flower by the path.

neighbors.heading: don't stand by
neighbors.text: Today people of another faith came to the Guru for help, and he did not send them away. The Torah sets a line among its laws of holiness: "neither shalt thou stand idly by the blood of thy neighbour: I am the LORD." The rabbis read it as a duty to step in when someone is in danger.
neighbors.difference: The verse is a commandment for every Jew, part of the law. Guru Tegh Bahadur's stand is remembered as one person's choice to protect a faith that wasn't his own, which Sikhs honor as martyrdom.
neighbors.shared: someone else's trouble can still be yours to answer.

neighbors.heading: freedom of conscience, for all
neighbors.text: Today the pandits came to a Guru whose path wasn't theirs, asking help to keep their own. People of many beliefs, and none, have reached the same conviction. After the Second World War, the nations wrote it down: everyone has the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion, to keep it or change it, and to practice it alone or together.
neighbors.difference: The Declaration is a shared promise between nations, grounded in human dignity, with no God named. Sikhs see Guru Tegh Bahadur's stand as rooted in faith, a duty before God to protect the conscience of others.
neighbors.shared: your freedom to believe is safest when you guard someone else's.
neighbors.sources: Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948), Article 18 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: you will find me steadfast
neighbors.text: Today a nine-year-old saw what was needed and said: who could be worthier than you, father? The Qur'an tells of a son just as ready. Abraham tells his boy of a dream that he must sacrifice him, and asks what he thinks. The son answers: "O my father! Do that which thou art commanded. Allah willing, thou shalt find me of the steadfast."
neighbors.difference: In the Qur'an, God stops the sacrifice and ransoms the son, and Muslims remember it each year at Eid al-Adha. Guru Tegh Bahadur's road really did lead to his death, for people outside his own community.
neighbors.shared: a child's courage can steady the grown-ups around them.

neighbors.heading: the boy who wouldn't bend
neighbors.text: Today a boy of nine spoke the hardest true thing in the room. Hindus tell of another brave child: Prahlada, son of a demon king who demanded to be worshipped. Prahlada kept praying to Vishnu, through threats and through fire, and would not bend. Many Hindus remember him each spring at Holi, when bonfires recall the fire that could not burn him.
neighbors.difference: Prahlada stood against his father's demand, and Vishnu came to save him. Gobind Rai stood with his father, offering him for others' freedom, and no rescue came; Sikhs remember it as the cost of courage.
neighbors.shared: sometimes the bravest person in the room is the youngest.
neighbors.sources: Bhagavata Purana, book 7 (paraphrase) · Holika Dahan at Holi (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the moon from behind clouds
neighbors.text: Today forty men who had walked away came back, and the Guru tore up the paper of their leaving. The Dhammapada has a line for anyone who turns around: "He who formerly was reckless and afterwards became sober, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds." The past is real. It just isn't the whole sky.
neighbors.difference: In the Buddha's teaching, no one tears up the record: the change comes by one's own effort, and actions still bear their fruit. The forty were freed by the Guru's grace, the paper torn by his own hand.
neighbors.shared: coming back counts, no matter how far you went.

neighbors.heading: while he was yet far off
neighbors.text: Today forty who had deserted came back, and the Guru tore up the paper they'd signed. Jesus told of a son who left home and wasted everything, then came back hoping only to be a servant. "But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him."
neighbors.difference: In the parable, the son comes home to a feast and lives on; Christians hear in it God's welcome for sinners who return. The forty came back and gave their lives, and Sikhs remember them every day in Ardas.
neighbors.shared: the door stays open for the one who walked out.

neighbors.heading: tutti fratelli
neighbors.text: Today Bhai Kanhaiya gave water to the wounded of both sides. In 1859 a Swiss businessman, Henry Dunant, came upon the battlefield of Solferino and joined the townswomen nursing the wounded of every army. Their phrase was tutti fratelli: all are brothers. His book about it helped spark the Red Cross, which serves the wounded of every side.
neighbors.difference: Dunant's work grew into treaties and a neutral organization, kept by law. Bhai Kanhaiya's answer was devotion: in every face, he said, he saw only his Guru, and his seva grew into a community, the Sevapanthis.
neighbors.shared: a wounded person is a person first, whatever side they're on.
neighbors.sources: Henry Dunant, A Memory of Solferino (1862) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: if thy enemy thirst
neighbors.text: Today Bhai Kanhaiya carried water to the wounded on both sides, and the Guru gave him balm too. Saint Paul wrote it plainly: "But if thy enemy be hungry, give him to eat; if he thirst, give him to drink." And Jesus told of a Samaritan who found a stranger beaten by the road, "and going up to him, bound up his wounds."
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, the enemy and the stranger are neighbors because Christ loves each of them. Bhai Kanhaiya said he saw only his Guru in every face; the root is different, and the hands do the same work.
neighbors.shared: a cup of water doesn't check which side you're on.

neighbors.heading: hearing comes first
neighbors.text: Today kirtan began not with singing but with listening. Hindus use the same word, kirtan, for singing God's names together. The Bhagavata Purana lists nine ways of devotion, and the first two are shravanam, hearing about God, and kirtanam, singing. Before the singing, the ears.
neighbors.difference: Hindu kirtan often sings the names of God in forms like Krishna or Rama, with a leader and a responding crowd. Sikh kirtan sings the hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib, set in their ragas.
neighbors.shared: the first step toward the sacred is simply listening.

neighbors.heading: hear, O Israel
neighbors.text: Today the practice was only your ears. A central line of Jewish prayer begins the same way: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." Shema means hear. Jews say it morning and night, and many cover their eyes while saying it, to listen with nothing else in the way.
neighbors.difference: The Shema is spoken, a declaration and a commandment, not a song. Kirtan is music, sung in a raga, and the listening is to the Guru's hymns. Both begin with the ears, and both turn toward the One.
neighbors.shared: before you speak to the One, you listen.
neighbors.sources: Deuteronomy 6:4 (JPS 1917) · Talmud, Berakhot 13b, covering the eyes (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: for his mercy endureth
neighbors.text: Today the sangat sang back what the singers led. One psalm is built for that: every verse of Psalm 136 ends with the same answer, "for his mercy endureth for ever." Many churches still pray psalms this way, a leader with the line and the whole room with the refrain. A child's voice next to a grandfather's, on the same words.
neighbors.difference: Christian psalm-singing comes from the Hebrew Bible, prayed through Christ in the church. Kirtan sings the Gurus' hymns in their ragas, with the Guru Granth Sahib present in the room.
neighbors.shared: when one voice falters, the room carries the line.

neighbors.heading: say what he says
neighbors.text: Today the sangat answered the singers line by line. Muslims have a call and answer too. When the adhan, the call to prayer, rings out, the Prophet taught those who hear it to repeat it after the caller, line by line, quietly, wherever they stand. A kitchen, a street, a car at a light, all answering the same words.
neighbors.difference: The adhan is a call, not a song: chanted by one voice, without instruments, to gather people for prayer. Kirtan is music, sung with harmonium and tabla, and the answering is itself the worship.
neighbors.shared: faith sounds different when many voices give the same answer.
neighbors.sources: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Call to Prayer (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a throne for a King
neighbors.text: Today the roti came into cupped hands, open and humble. Catholics know that gesture at Communion. In the fourth century, Saint Cyril of Jerusalem taught new Christians how to receive: make your left hand a throne for your right, since it is about to receive a King, and hollow your palm to hold it. Many receive on the tongue instead.
neighbors.difference: Catholics believe the host they receive is Christ himself, his body. Karah prashad is blessed food, and langar a shared meal; Sikhs receive both from the Guru's hand, as grace.
neighbors.shared: some gifts are best received with open hands.

neighbors.heading: the bowl held out
neighbors.text: Today the servers walked the rows, and people received with cupped hands. Buddhist monks and nuns live by that gesture. On the morning alms round, they walk quietly with a bowl, and lay people place food in it. The monk doesn't ask or choose, just receives. And the giver often bows, grateful for the chance to give.
neighbors.difference: On the alms round, the monastic receives and the lay person gives, and giving is a way to make merit. In langar, everyone is guest and server by turns, and what's received is understood as grace.
neighbors.shared: receiving well is a kindness too.

neighbors.heading: I will awake the dawn
neighbors.text: Today's hour was amrit vela, the nectar hour before dawn. A psalm sings it: "Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery and harp; I will awake the dawn." The code of Jewish law opens in that spirit: rise like a lion to serve your Creator, so that you wake the dawn, not the dawn you. Many Jews begin with a short thank-you before getting out of bed.
neighbors.difference: Shacharit, the Jewish morning prayer, can be said through the morning, with fixed words, often with a quorum of ten. Amrit vela is the dark before dawn itself, given to the Name and its greatness.
neighbors.shared: the first minutes of the day can belong to something bigger.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 57:9 (JPS 1917; 57:8 in many Bibles) · Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 1:1 (paraphrase) · Modeh Ani (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a dawn in me
neighbors.text: Today was about the hour before sunrise, when nothing has made a claim on you yet. Henry David Thoreau, in his cabin by Walden Pond, got up early and bathed in the pond, and called it a religious exercise. He wrote: "Morning is when I am awake and there is a dawn in me."
neighbors.difference: Thoreau's morning was wakefulness itself, alert to nature, with no set prayer and no named God. Amrit vela fills the early dark with the Name, as Japji asks: contemplate the true Name and its greatness.
neighbors.shared: an early hour, kept on purpose, wakes something up in you.
neighbors.sources: Thoreau, Walden (1854), "Where I Lived, and What I Lived For" · Japji, pauri 4, Ang 2 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: at fixed hours
neighbors.text: Today's word was Nitnem: set prayers at dawn, at sunset and before sleep, the same words every day. Muslims know that rhythm well. The Qur'an says: "Lo! worship at fixed hours hath been enjoined on the believers." Five times a day, from dawn to night, the call goes out, and the day is stitched together by prayer.
neighbors.difference: Salat is five set prayers with bowing and prostration, facing Mecca, in Arabic. Nitnem gathers at three times in the day, recited or listened to, with the Gurus' hymns as the words.
neighbors.shared: a day shaped by prayer has places to come back to.

neighbors.heading: the joining of the day
neighbors.text: Today the Sikh day opened three doors with the Guru's words. Traditional Hindu practice keeps a rhythm like it, called sandhya, the joining: prayers at the day's turning points, dawn, noon and dusk. At its heart is the Gayatri mantra from the Rig Veda, asking that the light of the divine sun awaken our minds.
neighbors.difference: Sandhya centers on the Gayatri, offerings of water, and the meeting of light and dark at the day's edges. Nitnem's three times are given to whole hymns of the Gurus, from Japji at dawn to Kirtan Sohila at night.
neighbors.shared: the same words, day after day, wear a path in the mind.
neighbors.sources: Rig Veda 3.62.10, the Gayatri mantra (paraphrase) · sandhyavandanam (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: one sleeps easily
neighbors.text: Today's bani was for bedtime: Kirtan Sohila, a song of trust before letting go. Buddhists end the day with a wish too: loving-kindness, metta, sent out to every being, near and far. The Buddha listed what it brings, and the first two are simple: one sleeps easily, and one wakes easily.
neighbors.difference: Metta is a wish sent outward, to all beings, without praising a Creator. Sohila praises God, and pictures death itself as the soul's wedding day.
neighbors.shared: go to sleep with a good wish, and the night feels kinder.

neighbors.heading: depart in peace
neighbors.text: Today's bedtime bani is also sung at funerals: sleep and death in one song. Christian night prayer holds that too. At Compline and Evensong, churches sing the words of Simeon, who had been promised he would see the Messiah before he died: "Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word." And a psalm: "I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep."
neighbors.difference: For Christians, that peace rests on Christ, whom Simeon held as a baby, and on the hope of resurrection. Sohila pictures death as a wedding, the soul meeting the Lord it has longed for.
neighbors.shared: lying down each night can be a small practice in trust.

neighbors.heading: one thought for the day
neighbors.text: Today the Granth fell open, and the verse on the page became the word for the day. The Stoic Seneca gave his friend Lucilius a habit like it: read widely, but each day choose one thought and digest it thoroughly, something to carry against hard things. Then he shared his own for that day, a line borrowed from Epicurus.
neighbors.difference: Seneca chose his thought himself, by judgment. The hukamnama isn't chosen by anyone: Sikhs receive it as the Guru speaking to the sangat that day.
neighbors.shared: one line, carried all day, can steady you.
neighbors.sources: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 2 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: take up and read
neighbors.text: Today a book fell open and gave the day its word. Saint Augustine's turning point came that way. Weeping in a garden, he heard a child's voice nearby chanting, "Take up and read; Take up and read." He opened Saint Paul's letters, read the first passage his eyes fell on, and the darkness of doubt lifted.
neighbors.difference: For Augustine it was one moment, not a daily rite. Catholics hear Scripture each day through readings set by a calendar; the hukamnama is taken fresh each morning, wherever the Granth falls open.
neighbors.shared: sometimes the word you need is the one you didn't pick.

neighbors.heading: lamps for a homecoming
neighbors.text: Today Sikhs lit lamps for a Guru who walked out of prison with fifty-two others. Hindus light lamps the same season for their own homecoming story. Tradition tells that when Rama returned to Ayodhya after his exile and his victory over Ravana, the city lined its streets with lamps. Diwali means a row of lamps.
neighbors.difference: For many Hindus, Diwali also honors Lakshmi, the goddess of fortune, and celebrates light over darkness. Bandi Chhor remembers a Guru who refused to be free alone. Same nights, same small flames, each for its own story.
neighbors.shared: a lit lamp says welcome home.
neighbors.sources: Ramayana tradition of Rama's return to Ayodhya (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: redeeming the captive
neighbors.text: Today's lamps remember a Guru who wouldn't leave prison unless the others came too. Jewish law gives that impulse a name: pidyon shvuyim, redeeming captives. Maimonides wrote that no commandment is greater, because a captive suffers hunger, thirst and danger all at once. And Isaiah speaks of one sent "to proclaim liberty to the captives."
neighbors.difference: In Jewish law, freeing captives is a community duty, often paid for with ransom raised together. Guru Hargobind's release of the fifty-two came by his own refusal to leave without them; tradition says each held a tassel of his cloak.
neighbors.shared: freedom means more when nobody gets left behind.
neighbors.sources: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Gifts to the Poor 8:10 (paraphrase) · Isaiah 61:1 (JPS 1917)

neighbors.heading: pray without ceasing
neighbors.text: Today's word was jap: repeat, remember, until the Name lives in your bones. Saint Paul gave Christians three words for it: "Pray without ceasing." Many Eastern Christians answer with the Jesus Prayer, one short line said again and again, often on a prayer rope: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me.
neighbors.difference: The Jesus Prayer calls on Jesus by name, whom Christians worship as the Son of God. Jap repeats Waheguru and the Gurus' words. Jesus also warned against "vain repetitions"; Sikh teaching also asks for remembering, not counting.
neighbors.shared: a few words, repeated with love, can become a home.

neighbors.heading: hearts find rest
neighbors.text: Today's word was jap: repeat, remember, a stairway of small steps. Muslims call remembrance dhikr, and many keep it on prayer beads, a short phrase of praise said again and again, like SubhanAllah, glory be to God. The Qur'an says why: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!"
neighbors.difference: Dhikr repeats Arabic phrases and names of God from the Qur'an and the Prophet's teaching. Jap repeats Waheguru and the Gurus' hymns. Teachers in both stress the heart remembering, not only the count.
neighbors.shared: the heart settles on what it keeps coming back to.

items.lessonTitle: Pauri 2, meaning: all within the order

neighbors.heading: now not I
neighbors.text: Today's pauri ended: whoever understands the order doesn't say I, I. Saint Paul wrote about the I stepping aside too: "And I live, now not I; but Christ liveth in me." And Catholics pray that same surrender every day in the Our Father: "Thy will be done."
neighbors.difference: For Paul, the I makes room for a person, Christ, living within. The pauri speaks of understanding the hukam, God's order, which holds everything; then the constant I goes quiet.
neighbors.shared: the loud I gets quieter when you see the bigger picture.

neighbors.heading: not mine, not me
neighbors.text: Today the pauri said that whoever understands the order stops saying I, I. The Buddha taught his first disciples to look at the body, feelings and thoughts and see each one this way: this is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Tradition says they were set free while listening.
neighbors.difference: The Buddha taught not-self without pointing to a Creator's order. Sikhs see the I go quiet inside God's hukam, with each soul a spark of the divine light.
neighbors.shared: a lighter I leaves more room for everyone else.

neighbors.heading: prayer before the day
neighbors.text: Today the Japji said: come in the early hours, and bring attention, not payment. Jews know that hour. A psalm says: "O LORD, in the morning shalt Thou hear my voice; in the morning will I order my prayer unto Thee, and will look forward." Jews pray Shacharit, the morning prayer, and the rabbis trace it to Abraham, who rose early to stand before God.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the amrit vela is for remembering the Name, and the pauri says grace opens the door. For Jews, morning prayer is a commandment with set words, one of three daily prayers, said facing Jerusalem.
neighbors.shared: the first quiet of the day belongs to something bigger.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 5:4 (JPS 1917; 5:3 in many Bibles) · Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 26b (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a dawn in me
neighbors.text: Today the Japji pointed to the quiet before dawn. Henry David Thoreau, living alone by Walden Pond, felt its pull too. He called every morning a cheerful invitation, and wrote: "Morning is when I am awake and there is a dawn in me." For him the clock mattered less than the waking: being awake on the inside.
neighbors.difference: The amrit vela turns toward the One and the Name, and the door is opened by grace. Thoreau looks to nature and his own wakefulness; he names no Guru and asks for no grace.
neighbors.shared: the quiet before the day has something to give you.
neighbors.sources: Henry David Thoreau, Walden (1854), "Where I Lived, and What I Lived For"

items.lessonTitle: Pauri 8, meaning: the power of listening

neighbors.heading: we hear, and we obey
neighbors.text: Today the Japji said: by listening, pain and wrongdoing are wiped away, and next comes mannai, trusting. The Qur'an pairs two steps too. Believers say: "We hear, and we obey." And it praises those "who hear advice and follow the best thereof." In Islam, the word is meant to be heard: the Qur'an is recited aloud.
neighbors.difference: In the Japji, the listening is to the Name and the Guru's word, and it leads to trust. In Islam, the word heard is the Qur'an, Allah's own speech, and hearing leads to following its commands.
neighbors.shared: a life changes first through the ears, then through the heart.

neighbors.heading: hear, then reflect
neighbors.text: Today the Japji said listening changes everything, and trusting comes next. The Upanishads give a ladder too. The sage Yajnavalkya tells his wife: "Verily, the Self is to be seen, to be heard, to be perceived, to be marked, O Maitreyi!" Later teachers named the steps: shravana, hearing the teaching; manana, reflecting on it; nididhyasana, meditating until it's lived.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the listening is to the Name and Gurbani, and it opens by the Guru's grace. In this Upanishad, what's heard is teaching about the Self, the atman, to be known directly by the seeker.
neighbors.shared: first you listen, then you let it change you.
neighbors.sources: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4.5 (Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East) · the steps of shravana, manana, nididhyasana in Vedanta teaching (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a raft, not the shore
neighbors.text: Today the Japji said no paper, pen or writer can hold the state of the one who trusts; the scripture points past itself. The Buddha said something close about his own teaching. He compared it to a raft: built for crossing a river, not for carrying on your head once you're across. The teaching is for crossing over, not for clinging to.
neighbors.difference: The Japji says the state of trust is known only by the one who trusts the Name. The Buddha speaks of no Name and no Creator; the raft carries you to nibbana, freedom from craving.
neighbors.shared: the words are a way in, and the rest is lived.
neighbors.sources: Majjhima Nikaya 22, Alagaddupama Sutta, the simile of the raft (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: past all understanding
neighbors.text: Today the Japji said the state of the one who trusts can't be told; you only know it from inside, like water. Paul writes something close to the church at Philippi: "And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus." A peace you can't explain, only be kept by.
neighbors.difference: In the Japji, that untellable state comes through trusting the Name. For Paul, the peace is God's gift through Christ Jesus, at the center of Christian faith; it keeps the heart rather than being reached by it.
neighbors.shared: some peace is too big for words, and still you can live in it.

items.lessonTitle: Pauri 20, meaning: what washes the mind

neighbors.heading: whiter than snow
neighbors.text: Today the Japji climbed a ladder: water washes the body, soap the clothes, and the love of the Name washes the mind. Catholics pray the same picture in Psalm 50, the Miserere: "Wash me yet more from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin." And: "thou shalt wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow."
neighbors.difference: In the Japji, the mind is dyed in the color of the Name, and you still eat what you sow. Catholics believe sin is washed by God's mercy through Christ, given in baptism and in confession, through a priest's absolution.
neighbors.shared: a stained heart doesn't have to stay stained.

neighbors.heading: you sow, you eat
neighbors.text: Today the Japji said: you yourself sow, and you yourself eat. The psychologist William James said it about habit: "We are spinning our own fates, good or evil, and never to be undone." Every small act, he wrote, leaves its little mark, so the person you'll become is built from what you do today, again and again.
neighbors.difference: The Japji sets this beside grace: the Name can dye even a stained mind clean, and all moves by the Hukam. James describes how habit works in body and brain; he promises no washing from outside.
neighbors.shared: small seeds, planted daily, become the life you live in.
neighbors.sources: William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890), ch. 4, "Habit"

items.lessonTitle: Pauri 24, meaning: no end to praise

neighbors.heading: mouths full of song
neighbors.text: Today the Japji said: the more is said, the more there is, and praise never reaches the end. A psalm says: "Great is the LORD, and highly to be praised; and His greatness is unsearchable." And the Shabbat morning prayer Nishmat says that even if our mouths were full of song like the sea, we could never thank God enough.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs sing of the endless One in the Guru's hymns, and the pauri rests in grace, nadar. Jews praise the God of Israel in psalms and set prayers, and Nishmat thanks God for rescuing and sustaining His people.
neighbors.shared: there's always more to be thankful for than words can hold.

neighbors.heading: no end of glories
neighbors.text: Today the Japji said there's no end to the praises and no end to the One praised. In the Gita, Arjuna asks Krishna to name his glories. Krishna names many: the sun among lights, the Ganges among rivers. Then he stops. There is no end to them, he says; what he has told is only a small sample.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, Krishna, God come as a person, describes his own glories to a friend. For Sikhs, the One is never born in a body, and the Gurus praise the Formless, who alone knows His greatness.
neighbors.shared: wherever you look, there's more wonder than you can count.

neighbors.heading: put on kindness
neighbors.text: Today the Japji turned a yogi's outfit inward: contentment for earrings, meditation for ashes, faith for a staff. Paul dresses Christians the same way: "Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering." And above all these, he says, put on charity, love.
neighbors.difference: In the Japji, the inner outfit answers the yogis, and the mind is the field to win. For Paul, these virtues are the clothes of a new life in Christ, worn because "even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye."
neighbors.shared: the best thing you wear is how you treat people.

neighbors.heading: the best clothing
neighbors.text: Today the Japji traded a yogi's earrings and ashes for contentment and meditation. The Qur'an makes a similar turn: "O Children of Adam! We have revealed unto you raiment to conceal your shame, and splendid vesture, but the raiment of restraint from evil, that is best." Clothes are a gift. Goodness is the garment that counts most.
neighbors.difference: Guru Nanak speaks to yogis about their own gear, and calls all humanity the true order. The Qur'an speaks to all the children of Adam, and its best garment is taqwa, mindful awe of Allah.
neighbors.shared: the clothes no one can see are the ones people remember.

neighbors.heading: not by bread alone
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak told the yogis: let wisdom be your meal, and compassion the one who serves it. Jesus, hungry in the desert, said: "Not in bread alone doth man live, but in every word that proceedeth from the mouth of God." And when the crowds who came to hear him were hungry, he didn't only teach them. He fed them.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, wisdom is the meal and the One's note already sounds in every heart. For Catholics, the deepest food is Christ himself, the bread of life, received in the Eucharist.
neighbors.shared: the best food is handed over with a kind hand.

neighbors.heading: never eat without sharing
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak said wisdom is the meal, and compassion holds the ladle. The Buddha set wisdom and giving side by side too. He said that if people knew, as he knew, the fruit of giving and sharing, they wouldn't eat without sharing, not even their last mouthful, if someone were there to receive it.
neighbors.difference: Guru Nanak names a Giver and hears the One's note in every heart. The Buddha speaks of giving as training the heart to let go, with no Creator in the picture.
neighbors.shared: wisdom tastes best when someone is kind enough to share it.

items.lessonTitle: Pauri 33, meaning: no power of our own

neighbors.heading: not by my own hand
neighbors.text: Today the Japji said: no power to speak or keep silent, to live or die; the power is in the One's hand. Moses warns the people that once life is comfortable, they mustn't say in their hearts: "My power and the might of my hand hath gotten me this wealth." Remember instead, he says, it is God who gives the power to get it.
neighbors.difference: The Japji lands on equality: by themselves, no one is high or low. Deuteronomy speaks to Israel about its covenant and its land, reminding the people to keep God's commandments when life is good.
neighbors.shared: work hard, and stay humble about where the strength came from.

neighbors.heading: what's in your hands
neighbors.text: Today the Japji listed what isn't in our power, down to life and death. The Stoic teacher Epictetus, once a slave, opened his handbook the same way: "Of things some are in our power, and others are not." Not in our power, he says: the body, property, reputation. Peace begins when you stop grabbing at those.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus keeps one thing for us: our own judgments, desires and choices. The Japji goes further, saying even awareness and reflection aren't ours to command; the One holds the power, and acts.
neighbors.shared: letting go of what you can't hold leaves your hands free.

items.lessonTitle: The final salok: air, water, earth

neighbors.heading: from earth and water
neighbors.text: Today the Japji closed with a family: air the Guru, water the father, earth the great mother. The Qur'an speaks of earth and water too. Of the earth: "Thereof We created you, and thereunto We return you, and thence We bring you forth a second time." And of water: "We made every living thing of water."
neighbors.difference: The salok calls earth a mother and air a Guru, a family picture of creation. In the Qur'an, earth and water are signs of Allah, made by Him and serving Him, and never called parent or guide.
neighbors.shared: the ground under you and the water you drink are gifts.

neighbors.heading: earth is my mother
neighbors.text: Today the Japji called the earth the great mother. A long hymn to the Earth in the Atharva Veda says it in Sanskrit words still quoted today: mata bhumih, putro aham prithivyah. The earth is my mother; I am her child. Some Hindu families say a morning verse asking her pardon before their feet touch the ground.
neighbors.difference: In the hymn, Earth is Prithvi, honored as a goddess with her own praises. In Gurbani, earth as mother is a picture of creation's care; Sikhs worship only the One Creator, not the earth itself.
neighbors.shared: the earth that holds you up deserves a little tenderness back.
neighbors.sources: Atharva Veda 12.1.12, the hymn to the Earth (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Haumai: the disease with its own cure

neighbors.heading: the trouble with "mine"
neighbors.text: Today the Granth called haumai, I-me, a chronic disease with its cure inside. The Buddha also saw trouble in I and mine. The Dhammapada says: "'These sons belong to me, and this wealth belongs to me,' with such thoughts a fool is tormented. He himself does not belong to himself; how much less sons and wealth?"
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the cure is turning the I toward the One, by grace and the Guru's word. The Buddha teaches anatta, not-self: look closely and no lasting I is found, with no Creator in the picture.
neighbors.shared: life gets lighter when it stops being all about me.

neighbors.heading: he must increase
neighbors.text: Today the Granth said haumai, the I-me, is a long illness, and its cure lives inside it too. Christians know that turn. John the Baptist, watching people leave him for Jesus, said: "He must increase, but I must decrease." And Paul wrote: "I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me."
neighbors.difference: In the Granth, the I turns toward the One through the Name and the Guru's word. For Christians, the old self is healed through Christ, who died and rose, and the new life is Christ living in the believer.
neighbors.shared: there's freedom in not having to be the center.

neighbors.heading: name it to tame it
neighbors.text: Today the Granth said the first step with the five thieves is to know them: their faces, their habits. Psychology found something close. In brain-scan studies led by Matthew Lieberman, when people put a feeling into a word, like angry or afraid, the brain's alarm center calmed more than when they just looked. Naming a feeling loosens its grip.
neighbors.difference: The Granth calls them thieves who steal the nectar of the Name, and the guard is the Name and the Guru. The psychology names no enemy and no God; it only shows that labeling a feeling quiets it.
neighbors.shared: a feeling you can name is easier to live with.
neighbors.sources: Lieberman et al., "Putting Feelings Into Words," Psychological Science (2007) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the capital sins
neighbors.text: Today the Granth named five thieves living inside: lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride. Catholics keep a list too: the seven capital sins, pride, avarice, envy, wrath, lust, gluttony and sloth. The Church calls them capital because they're heads: other sins spring from them. And vices, it teaches, can be sorted by the virtues they oppose.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the five begin as natural energies that become thieves when they take over, and the Name guards the house. For Catholics, sin turns a person from God, and grace heals it, especially in confession.
neighbors.shared: knowing your own weak spots is the start of being free.

items.lessonTitle: Ask about the light, not the caste

neighbors.heading: an equal eye
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak said: recognize the light, don't ask about caste. The Gita has a line still quoted on this. The wise, Krishna says, look with an equal eye on a learned Brahmin, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and an outcaste. And near the end: the Lord dwells in the heart of every being.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, the equal eye belongs to the wise, and Hindu texts also describe varna, social orders that Hindus read in very different ways. The Gurus set caste aside in practice: one langar, one bowl of amrit.
neighbors.shared: the light in someone matters more than the label on them.

neighbors.heading: one father for all
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak said: recognize the light, don't ask about caste. The prophet Malachi asks: "Have we not all one father? Hath not one God created us?" And the Mishnah explains why God began with just one person: so that no one could ever say to another, my father is greater than yours.
neighbors.difference: Judaism keeps some lines of descent, like the kohanim, the priestly families, with roles in blessing and ritual. The Gurus set birth-groups aside and gave every Khalsa Sikh one name: Singh or Kaur.
neighbors.shared: nobody's family tree is taller than anyone else's.

neighbors.heading: the other cheek
neighbors.text: Today Sheikh Farid said: if someone strikes you, don't strike back; go home in peace. Jesus said: "whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also." And Paul wrote to the church in Rome: "Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good."
neighbors.difference: Sikhs hold Farid's go home beside Kabir's warrior who defends the helpless. Christians read Jesus' words in different ways too: some as a call to refuse all violence, others as a word about personal revenge.
neighbors.shared: the fight ends sooner when you don't carry it home.

neighbors.heading: repel it with better
neighbors.text: Today Sheikh Farid, a Muslim Sufi whose verses sit in the Guru Granth Sahib, said: don't strike back. His own scripture says: "Repel the evil deed with one which is better, then lo! he, between whom and thee there was enmity (will become) as though he was a bosom friend."
neighbors.difference: Here the doors overlap: Farid is a Muslim voice inside the Sikh scripture. Muslims read his kind of mercy beside the Qur'an and the Prophet's example; Sikhs sing his verses as gurbani, beside the Gurus' own hymns.
neighbors.shared: kindness can turn an enemy into a friend.

neighbors.heading: a rule for living
neighbors.text: Today rehat meant a way of living, not a checklist to earn God's favor. Catholic monks and nuns live by a rule too. Saint Benedict wrote his Rule as a school for the Lord's service, hoping to set down nothing harsh or burdensome. Prayer, work, meals and sleep all get a shape, so the whole day can turn toward God.
neighbors.difference: The Rehat Maryada is for every Sikh, kept in different degrees, at home and at work. Benedict's Rule is for monks and nuns who take vows in a monastery; other Catholics keep the Church's own precepts.
neighbors.shared: a good rule is a shape for love, not a cage.

neighbors.heading: a training you take on
neighbors.text: Today rehat meant a way of living that turns teaching into habit. Buddhists keep five precepts, and their wording is worth noticing. Each begins: I undertake the training rule to abstain from... then taking life, taking what isn't given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and intoxicants. Not a command from above. A training you take on yourself.
neighbors.difference: Rehat flows from the Guru's teaching and, for those who take amrit, comes with the five Ks. Buddhist precepts are taken on by the person, with no Creator giving them; the Buddha taught them as training, not as divine law.
neighbors.shared: a good way of living is practiced, not just believed.
neighbors.sources: The five precepts (pancasila), as chanted in Pali (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a sign upon thy hand
neighbors.text: Today the kara sat on the wrist, asking: what are these hands doing? Jews know a sign on the arm. The Shema says: "And thou shalt bind them for a sign upon thy hand, and they shall be for frontlets between thine eyes." On weekday mornings, observant Jews wind tefillin, small leather boxes holding these words, on the arm and head.
neighbors.difference: The kara is worn all day, plain steel, a circle for the One without end. Tefillin are put on for weekday morning prayer, and hold handwritten verses of the Torah inside.
neighbors.shared: what you wear on your arm can remind your hands who they serve.

neighbors.heading: a cue on your wrist
neighbors.text: Today the kara caught the light every time the hand moved. Psychology has a name for that: a cue. In Peter Gollwitzer's research on if-then plans, people who tied a goal to a concrete cue, if I see this, then I'll do that, followed through more often than people with good intentions alone. A reminder you can see helps.
neighbors.difference: The kara is an article of faith, a circle for the endless One and a bond with the Guru. A cue in psychology is a tool anyone can choose, for any goal, sacred or ordinary.
neighbors.shared: a small reminder can keep a big promise.

neighbors.heading: begin not hostilities
neighbors.text: Today dharam yudh meant a fight with limits, and Bhai Ghanaiya gave water to every wounded man. The Qur'an sets a limit too: "Fight in the way of Allah against those who fight against you, but begin not hostilities. Lo! Allah loveth not aggressors." Early tradition adds: don't kill women, children or the old, and don't cut down fruit trees.
neighbors.difference: Sikh rules of righteous war come mostly from tradition and history, not from one list in scripture. In Islam, the limits rest on the Qur'an and hadith, and scholars built them into a detailed body of law.
neighbors.shared: even in a fight, the other person never stops being a person.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 2:190 (Pickthall 1930) · Abu Bakr's instructions to his army, in the Muwatta of Malik, Book of Jihad (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: rules at Kurukshetra
neighbors.text: Today dharam yudh meant a fight with limits. The Mahabharata tells of rules agreed before its great war at Kurukshetra: fight only an equal; don't strike someone who is fleeing, who has surrendered, or who has no weapon; don't harm drummers or those carrying supplies. And it is honest: in the story the rules are broken, and grief follows.
neighbors.difference: The Mahabharata sets righteous war inside the dharma of the warrior class. Sikh tradition opens the saint-soldier's path to anyone who takes amrit, whatever their birth, and its rules come from the Gurus' tradition.
neighbors.shared: how you fight says as much as why you fight.

neighbors.heading: the greatest conqueror
neighbors.text: Today the Japji said: conquer your own mind, and you've conquered the world. The Dhammapada says it in battle words: "If one man conquer in battle a thousand times thousand men, and if another conquer himself, he is the greatest of conquerors." In Buddhist teaching, the real enemies are inside: greed, hatred and delusion.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs fight the five thieves with the Name, the sangat and the Guru's grace, beside the saint-soldier's duty to defend. The Buddha's way is training the mind, with no Creator to call on; the victory is freedom from craving.
neighbors.shared: the hardest win, and the best one, is over yourself.

neighbors.heading: the good that I would
neighbors.text: Today the Japji named the real battle: inside, against anger, greed and pride. Paul knew it well. "For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do." Then he cries out for rescue, and answers himself: "I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord."
neighbors.difference: Sikhs fight the five thieves day by day, with the Name, the sangat and the Guru's grace. For Paul, the rescue comes through Christ's death and rising, and through the Spirit living in the believer.
neighbors.shared: you're not the only one fighting yourself, and that's a comfort.

items.lessonTitle: The Dal Khalsa and the council

neighbors.heading: good to the Holy Ghost and to us
neighbors.text: Today Sikhs gathered before the Guru Granth Sahib to decide together, and the decision became the Guru's. The early Church did something close. When the apostles and elders met in Jerusalem over a hard question, they talked it through, then wrote: "For it hath seemed good to the Holy Ghost and to us." Catholics still gather bishops in councils.
neighbors.difference: A gurmata is made by the whole assembly in the Guru's presence and sealed with Ardas. In the Catholic Church, councils gather the bishops with the Pope, and Catholics believe the Holy Spirit guides their teaching.
neighbors.shared: decide together, in front of what you all respect.

neighbors.heading: the potluck of minds
neighbors.text: Today a gurmata held because the whole assembly agreed. The philosopher Aristotle argued for something similar. Many people, each with a piece of good sense, can judge better together than a few of the best alone, he wrote, the way a feast where many bring a dish beats a dinner paid for out of one purse.
neighbors.difference: A gurmata's weight comes from the Guru's presence and the prayer that seals it. Aristotle's case is about human judgment alone: pooled good sense, with no sacred presence needed.
neighbors.shared: the whole table usually sees more than one chair.

neighbors.heading: holding fast to truth
neighbors.text: Today Sikh volunteers at Guru ka Bagh were beaten and didn't strike back, and Gandhi cheered their earlier win. Gandhi called his own way satyagraha, holding fast to truth, and rooted it in ahimsa, non-harm. The Yoga Sutras say that when someone is firmly grounded in non-harm, hostility falls away in their presence.
neighbors.difference: Gandhi held non-violence as a creed for nearly every situation. The Akalis took a vow of non-violence for their campaign, and Sikh teaching also keeps the sword as a last resort to defend the helpless.
neighbors.shared: standing firm without striking back takes deep courage.
neighbors.sources: Yoga Sutras 2.35 (paraphrase) · M. K. Gandhi, Hind Swaraj (1909), on satyagraha (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the midwives said no
neighbors.text: Today Sikh volunteers held firm without violence until the gurdwaras came home. The Torah's first story of refusal is quiet too. Pharaoh ordered two midwives, Shiphrah and Puah, to kill the Hebrew baby boys. "But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men-children alive." No weapons. Just a firm no.
neighbors.difference: The Akali bands protested in public, in great numbers, under a vow of non-violence. The midwives' refusal was quiet and personal, and Jewish law also permits self-defense; non-violence isn't made a rule for every case.
neighbors.shared: a firm, peaceful no can be stronger than a fist.

neighbors.heading: cast down, not destroyed
neighbors.text: Today chardi kala meant grief and getting up at the same time, again and again. Paul, beaten and on the move, wrote: "We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair; Persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed." Not pretending it's fine. Getting up anyway.
neighbors.difference: Chardi kala rises through the Name and the will of the One, asked for in every Ardas. Paul's hope rests on Jesus' death and rising: he carries Christ's dying, he says, so Christ's life can show too.
neighbors.shared: knocked down isn't the same as finished.

neighbors.heading: with hardship, ease
neighbors.text: Today families who lost everything in 1947 started over with rising spirits. The Qur'an speaks to a heavy heart: "But lo! with hardship goeth ease, Lo! with hardship goeth ease." Said twice, so it sinks in. And the Islamic calendar counts from a fresh start: the Hijra, when the Prophet and his companions left Mecca for Medina.
neighbors.difference: Chardi kala is a spirit Sikhs ask for in every Ardas, through the Name. In the Qur'an, the promise of ease comes from Allah, and Muslims meet hardship with sabr, patient trust in Him.
neighbors.shared: the hard part isn't the whole story.

neighbors.heading: the labor of their hands
neighbors.text: Today Sikh men milled lumber far from home, living kirat karni, honest work with their own hands. Catholics honor work too. Saint Benedict wrote that idleness is the enemy of the soul, and that monks are truly monks when they live by the labor of their hands. And the Gospels remember Jesus as the carpenter's son.
neighbors.difference: Kirat karni sits beside remembering the Name and sharing what you earn. For Benedict, work is woven between set hours of prayer in a monastery, and the Church teaches that work shares in God's own creating.
neighbors.shared: honest work, done well, has its own quiet holiness.
neighbors.sources: Rule of Saint Benedict, ch. 48 (paraphrase) · Matthew 13:55 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: right livelihood
neighbors.text: Today Sikh men milled lumber in Canada, living kirat karni, an honest living by their own work. The Buddha put work on his path too. Right livelihood is one step of the Eightfold Path, and he named five trades to avoid: trading in weapons, in people, in meat, in intoxicants and in poisons.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, honest work goes with remembering the One and sharing with others. In the Buddha's teaching, right livelihood means earning without causing harm, as training on the path to freedom, with no Creator involved.
neighbors.shared: how you earn your bread is part of who you are.

neighbors.heading: bread to the hungry
neighbors.text: Today the langar traveled, from Amritsar's kitchen to floods and borders. Jews hear a prophet's call. Isaiah says the fast God wants is this: "Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house?" And early in the Passover seder comes an invitation: let all who are hungry come and eat.
neighbors.difference: Langar is a free kitchen at the gurdwara, open to all, everyone on the same floor. Jewish giving is tzedakah, a commanded duty of justice, and the seder's invitation is spoken at a family table at Passover.
neighbors.shared: a hungry person is a guest, not a stranger.
neighbors.sources: Isaiah 58:7 (JPS 1917) · Passover Haggadah, Ha Lachma Anya (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: giving feeds the giver
neighbors.text: Today the langar went out to floods and borders. Psychologists have measured part of why that feels right. In a study led by Elizabeth Dunn, people were handed money to spend by evening. Those told to spend it on someone else ended the day happier than those told to spend it on themselves. Giving fed the giver too.
neighbors.difference: Langar is seva, service offered to the Guru, seeing the one light in everyone. The study names no God and no duty; it only shows giving lifts the giver's mood, which Sikhs wouldn't call the reason.
neighbors.shared: feeding someone else has a way of filling you up.
neighbors.sources: Dunn, Aknin & Norton, "Spending Money on Others Promotes Happiness," Science (2008) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: that ye may know one another
neighbors.text: Today Guru Arjan sang: no one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger. The Qur'an speaks to all people: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." Different peoples aren't made to stay strangers. They're made to get to know each other.
neighbors.difference: Guru Arjan finds no stranger because the one God is present in everyone, seen in holy company. The Qur'an speaks of Allah as Creator of all, distinct from creation, and honors people by their conduct, not their tribe.
neighbors.shared: a stranger is just someone you haven't met yet.

neighbors.heading: the earth is one family
neighbors.text: Today Guru Arjan sang: no one is a stranger. A Sanskrit verse from the Maha Upanishad says it this way: counting "this one is mine, that one is a stranger" is for small minds. For the large-hearted, vasudhaiva kutumbakam: the whole earth is one family.
neighbors.difference: The verse grounds it in a large heart, and some Hindu schools add that one Self lives in all. Guru Arjan's reason is the one God present in everyone, seen in holy company, not that each person is God.
neighbors.shared: the whole earth can feel like one big family table.

neighbors.heading: may all beings be happy
neighbors.text: Today the Ardas ended with sarbat da bhala: the good of all, even those who did the hurting. Buddhists chant a wish just as wide. The Metta Sutta asks that all beings be happy and at ease: the weak and the strong, the seen and unseen, near and far, born and yet to be born, loved the way a mother guards her only child.
neighbors.difference: The Ardas asks the One for everyone's good, by your will, leaving its shape to the Giver. Metta is a wish grown in the heart, addressed to no Creator; the practice changes the one who wishes.
neighbors.shared: the best wishes are the ones with no one left out.

neighbors.heading: pray for them
neighbors.text: Today the Ardas asked for the good of all, including those who did the hurting. Jesus asked the same of his followers: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you."
neighbors.difference: Sarbat da bhala grows from seeing the one light in every person. Christians pray for enemies following Jesus, who, the Gospel says, prayed on the cross for the ones crucifying him.
neighbors.shared: the widest prayer leaves no one out, not even the one who hurt you.

neighbors.heading: living outside the clock
neighbors.text: Today Jaap bowed to akaal, the One beyond time and death. A philosopher reached for timelessness too. Ludwig Wittgenstein wrote: "If by eternity is understood not endless temporal duration but timelessness, then he lives eternally who lives in the present." For him, the timeless isn't somewhere far away. It's found in a moment you stop counting.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the Timeless is a Being, Akal Purakh, the One you can bow to and love. Wittgenstein named no Being; he was describing a way of living, wholly in the present.
neighbors.shared: not everything that matters is on the clock.

neighbors.heading: from eternity to eternity
neighbors.text: Today Jaap bowed to akaal, the One no clock can touch. Catholics pray to a God beyond time too. A psalm sings: "Before the mountains were made, or the earth and the world was formed; from eternity and to eternity thou art God." And Peter's letter adds that with the Lord, one day is as a thousand years.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs call the Timeless ajooni, never born into a body. Catholics believe the eternal Son of God entered time, born of Mary as Jesus, while remaining fully God.
neighbors.shared: underneath every ticking clock, something holds steady.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 89:2 (Douay-Rheims; Psalm 90:2 in many Bibles) · 2 Peter 3:8 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: i carry what they need
neighbors.text: Today Jaap called the One rozi dihind, the giver of daily bread. Hindus hear a promise like that from Krishna in the Bhagavad Gita. In paraphrase: to those who worship me, thinking of no other, always devoted, I bring what they lack and keep safe what they have. The day's portion, in that picture, is held by loving hands.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, Krishna speaks as God in a human form, face to face with his friend Arjuna. Sikhs praise a Provider who is never born, and answer the gift with honest work and a shared kitchen.
neighbors.shared: every plate of food is a gift someone gave.

neighbors.heading: who feeds all
neighbors.text: Today Jaap called the One the giver of daily bread. Jews say a psalm with the same picture in daily prayer: "The eyes of all wait for Thee, And Thou givest them their food in due season. Thou openest Thy hand, And satisfiest every living thing with favour." And the grace after meals blesses God, who feeds all.
neighbors.difference: In Jewish prayer, the One who feeds all is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who gave the Torah to Israel. Jaap praises the Provider among the many names of the Timeless One, beyond every people.
neighbors.shared: even an ordinary lunch is a reason to say thank you.

neighbors.heading: whom shall i fear?
neighbors.text: Today Jaap praised abhai, the Fearless One, and Sikhs hope to grow fearless too. Christians sing a psalm with that same courage: "The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?" And John's letter roots it in love: "There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear."
neighbors.difference: Sikhs praise fearlessness as part of God's own nature, nirbhau, and Sikhs grow toward it. Christians root their courage in being loved: God's love, shown in Jesus, casts the fear out.
neighbors.shared: love can make a frightened heart brave.

neighbors.heading: no fear upon them
neighbors.text: Today Jaap praised abhai, and Guru Tegh Bahadur taught: frighten no one, fear no one. The Qur'an speaks of a fearlessness given to those close to God: "Lo! verily the friends of Allah are (those) on whom fear (cometh) not, nor do they grieve." And believers under threat answered: "Allah is Sufficient for us!"
neighbors.difference: In the Qur'an, the friends of God are unafraid because they hold God alone in awe, taqwa. Sikhs praise fearlessness as part of the One's own nature, nirbhau, and grow toward it.
neighbors.shared: the one who trusts deeply can stand without fear.

neighbors.heading: without love, nothing
neighbors.text: Today the Tenth Guru weighed every holy parade and said: without love, not worth a seed. Paul set the same scale for Catholics: "And if I should distribute all my goods to feed the poor, and if I should deliver my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing." Charity there means love, the greatest of the three.
neighbors.difference: Catholics honor monks, nuns and fasting as good paths when love leads them. Sikh teaching favors the householder's life of family and work over the cave, while asking for the same love at the center.
neighbors.shared: love is what gives every practice its weight.

neighbors.heading: not the matted hair
neighbors.text: Today the Tenth Guru said hosts of yogis and ascetics weigh nothing without love. The Dhammapada also looks past outward show: "Not nakedness, not platted hair, not dirt, not fasting, or lying on the earth, not rubbing with dust, not sitting motionless, can purify a mortal who has not overcome desires."
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, what tips the empty scale is love for the Lord, given by grace. The Buddha points to a mind freed from craving, and his path doesn't rest on a creator God.
neighbors.shared: what's inside matters more than what anyone can see.

neighbors.heading: with all your heart
neighbors.text: Today the Tenth Guru said: those who loved, they found the Lord. Jews hear that promise in the prophet Jeremiah: "And ye shall seek Me, and find Me, when ye shall search for Me with all your heart." And the Shema, said morning and night, asks for that love: "thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thy heart."
neighbors.difference: Jewish love of God is lived through the Torah's commandments, the mitzvot, done with the heart. The Savaiye set outward rites aside and say love alone finds the Lord, shown in the Name and in service.
neighbors.shared: a whole heart that searches is not left empty.

neighbors.heading: love leads yonder
neighbors.text: Today the Tenth Guru said: those who loved, they found the Lord. The poet Rumi, read by seekers far beyond his own Sufi path, says love itself is the road: "Whether love be from this (earthly) side or from that (heavenly) side, in the end it leads us yonder." For him, even a human love can teach the heart the way.
neighbors.difference: Rumi was a Muslim mystic, and many seekers read him today as a teacher of love itself. The Savaiye's love is prem for the one Lord, lived out in a Sikh life of Name and service.
neighbors.shared: love is a road, and it goes somewhere.
neighbors.sources: Rumi, Masnavi, Book I, line 111 (Nicholson translation, 1926)

neighbors.heading: nearer than your pulse
neighbors.text: Today the Chaupai said the One knows what's inside every heart, and recognizes the pain of the good and the bad. The Qur'an speaks of that closeness: "We verily created man and We know what his soul whispereth to him, and We are nearer to him than his jugular vein." One of God's names is Al-Alim, the All-Knowing.
neighbors.difference: Muslims hold that God knows every heart while remaining wholly distinct from creation, never mixed into it. Sikh scripture speaks of the One's light also dwelling inside every heart, in every vessel.
neighbors.shared: you are known all the way through, and still held.

neighbors.heading: the inner ruler
neighbors.text: Today the Chaupai praised the One who knows what's inside every heart. Antarjami is a Hindu word too. In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, a sage describes, in paraphrase, the one who dwells within all beings, whom the beings do not know, who guides them from within: your Self, the inner ruler, the immortal. Krishna says the Lord dwells in every heart.
neighbors.difference: Hindu schools differ on whether that inner ruler is one with your deepest self, or close yet distinct. Sikhs speak of one light in every heart, and of the soul merging into the One by grace.
neighbors.shared: someone sees the ache you never told anyone.

neighbors.heading: the best riches
neighbors.text: Today the Anand said the true Name is my support, and it took away all my hunger. The Dhammapada speaks of a fullness that doesn't come from getting more: "Health is the greatest of gifts, contentedness the best riches; trust is the best of relationships, Nirvana the highest happiness." Peace there grows as craving quiets.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the hunger is stilled by the Name, a gift through the Guru, met with gratitude. Buddhists see the hunger itself as craving, which ends as it's understood and let go along the Buddha's path.
neighbors.shared: enough can be found, and it brings peace.

neighbors.heading: never hunger
neighbors.text: Today the Anand said the true Name takes away all hunger and brings peace to live in the mind. Christians remember these words of Jesus: "I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst." The hunger he means is the deep one, under every lunch.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, the bread of life is Jesus himself, met in faith and, for many, in communion. For Sikhs, the support is the Name, remembered and sung, given through the Guru's Word.
neighbors.shared: the deepest hunger can be filled.

neighbors.heading: the heart's reasons
neighbors.text: Today the Anand said: O restless mind, no one has found the One through cleverness. Blaise Pascal, a brilliant mathematician, reached the same wall: "The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know." For him, some of the deepest things are known the way you know you love someone, not by winning an argument.
neighbors.difference: Pascal trusted the heart to know, and still prized reason. The Anand says even the finding is a gift: the One is found by grace, through the Guru's Word, not by any faculty of ours.
neighbors.shared: some things are found by the heart, not by cleverness.

neighbors.heading: hidden from the clever
neighbors.text: Today the Anand said cleverness never found the One. Jesus thanked his Father for the same surprise: "I confess to thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to little ones." The Church teaches that faith is a gift of God.
neighbors.difference: Catholics hold that faith and reason are partners, and honor thinkers like Thomas Aquinas, while faith itself is God's gift through Christ. The Anand says the One is found by grace through the Guru's Word.
neighbors.shared: a humble heart sees what a clever one can miss.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 11:25 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 153, 159 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the same light within
neighbors.text: Today the Anand told the body: the Lord placed His light in you, and then you came into the world. Hindus hear a near echo in the Chandogya Upanishad. In paraphrase: the light that shines beyond this heaven, above everything, in the highest worlds, is the same light that shines within a person.
neighbors.difference: Some Hindu schools hear that inner light as your own true self, one with Brahman. For Sikhs, the light, jot, is placed in you by the Lord, and the soul longs to merge back into its source.
neighbors.shared: there's a light in you that you didn't have to earn.

neighbors.heading: the lamp of the LORD
neighbors.text: Today the Anand told the body: the Lord placed His light in you, and then you came into the world. A Hebrew proverb has its own lamp: "The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD, Searching all the inward parts." And Genesis tells how God breathed into the first person the breath of life.
neighbors.difference: In Jewish teaching, each person is made in God's image, yet remains a creature, not a part of God. Sikh scripture speaks of God's own light dwelling in every body, and of the soul merging back into that light.
neighbors.shared: every person carries a light worth honoring.

neighbors.heading: lighten our darkness
neighbors.text: Today Rehras packed provisions for the night as the day's work ends. Christians keep evening prayer too.
