One old evening prayer asks: "Lighten our darkness, we beseech thee, O Lord; and by thy great mercy defend us from all perils and dangers of this night." A psalm asks that lifted hands be "as the evening sacrifice."
neighbors.difference: Christians pray these evening words for the love of Jesus Christ, as the prayer itself ends. Rehras sings the Gurus' own hymns and closes, in many homes, with Ardas.
neighbors.shared: as the light goes, ask to be kept through the night.
neighbors.sources: Book of Common Prayer 1662, Evening Prayer, third collect · Psalm 141:2 (KJV)

neighbors.heading: prayer at sunset
neighbors.text: Today Rehras marked the end of the working day with prayer. Muslims pray as the light goes too: maghrib at sunset, and isha after dark. The Qur'an says: "Establish worship at the two ends of the day and in some watches of the night. Lo! good deeds annul ill deeds."
neighbors.difference: Muslim prayer at sunset is salah: set words in Arabic, with bows and prostrations toward Mecca. Rehras is the Gurus' hymns, recited or sung in the Guru's own languages.
neighbors.shared: put the day down, and turn toward God.

items.lessonTitle: This human body is your chance

neighbors.heading: now is the time
neighbors.text: Today Guru Arjan said: you've received this human body; this is your turn to meet the Lord. Paul writes with the same urgency: "Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation." And in the Hail Mary, Catholics ask for prayers "now and at the hour of our death."
neighbors.difference: Sikh teaching speaks of the soul passing through many lives, which makes a human birth rare. Catholics believe each person lives one earthly life, followed by judgment, which makes this one precious in its own way.
neighbors.shared: this life is a gift, and today counts.

neighbors.heading: a rare human birth
neighbors.text: Today Guru Arjan said: you have this human body, so now is your turn. Buddhists treasure a human life the same way. The Dhammapada says: "Difficult (to obtain) is the conception of men, difficult is the life of mortals, difficult is the hearing of the True Law." A human life is the rare chance to practice.
neighbors.difference: Both see many lives, and a precious human one. For Sikhs, the chance is to meet the Lord through the Name. Buddhists speak of awakening and the end of rebirth, along the Buddha's path, with no creator God.
neighbors.shared: you are here now, and that's a rare gift.

neighbors.heading: the young ravens
neighbors.text: Today Guru Arjan asked why the mind schemes, when even creatures in the rocks are fed. A psalm points to the same small mouths: "He giveth to the beast his food, And to the young ravens which cry." The Talmud remembers Hillel, who met each day trusting, in paraphrase: blessed be the Lord, day by day.
neighbors.difference: In the psalm, God's care is bound up with a covenant with Israel, a people. Guru Arjan speaks to each mind directly, and points to the true congregation and the Guru's grace as the way across.
neighbors.shared: you are cared for more than worry lets you see.

neighbors.heading: what's yours to carry
neighbors.text: Today Guru Arjan asked: why plot and scheme, mind, when your keeping is already cared for? The Stoic Epictetus gave anxious minds a sorting rule: "Of things some are in our power, and others are not." Do your part with what's yours, he taught, and stop wrestling with the rest. Much worry is a mind grabbing what it can't hold.
neighbors.difference: Guru Arjan's calm rests on trust in a loving Lord who feeds every creature. Epictetus found calm mainly in sorting what's up to us, though he too spoke of a providence ordering the world.
neighbors.shared: do your part, then let your shoulders drop.

neighbors.heading: signs of one Maker
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak said: the sun is one, the seasons are many. The Qur'an also reads the turning days as signs of one Maker: "And of His portents are the night and the day and the sun and the moon. Adore not the sun nor the moon; but adore Allah Who created them."
neighbors.difference: The Qur'an keeps a clear line between the Creator and the sun, a sign to read, never to worship. Guru Nanak says the many forms are the Creator's own, the One showing itself in all of them.
neighbors.shared: every changing season points back to one steady source.

neighbors.heading: one truth, many names
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak said the sun is one, the seasons many, and the Creator's forms are countless. The Rig Veda says something close. In paraphrase: truth is one; the wise call it by many names, Indra, Mitra, Varuna, Agni. And the Gayatri mantra, from the same Veda, turns toward the bright light of the sun.
neighbors.difference: Many Hindus honor the One through many deities and sacred images, each a doorway. Sikhs see the One in every form, yet worship no image; they worship through the Name and the Guru's Word.
neighbors.shared: the names change with the season; the light stays one.
neighbors.sources: Rig Veda 1.164.46 (paraphrase) · Rig Veda 3.62.10, the Gayatri mantra (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a city of bones
neighbors.text: Today the Sohila called the body a city crowded with desire and anger. The Dhammapada uses a city picture too: "After a stronghold has been made of the bones, it is covered with flesh and blood, and there dwell in it old age and death, pride and deceit." Buddhists also speak of three fires inside: greed, hatred and delusion.
neighbors.difference: The Sohila clears the city by humility, the holy company and God's grace. Buddhists cool the fires through their own practice, mindfulness and ethics, guided by the Buddha and the sangha, the community.
neighbors.shared: you don't have to clear the city alone.
neighbors.sources: Dhammapada 150 (Max Müller 1881) · the Fire Sermon, Samyutta Nikaya 35.28 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: from within
neighbors.text: Today the Sohila said desire and anger crowd the city of the body. Jesus pointed inside too: "For from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts." And Paul wrote of another law in his body, at war with his mind, and cried out: who will rescue me?
neighbors.difference: For Christians, the rescue comes through Jesus: Paul's cry ends in thanks to God through him. The Sohila points to bowing before the holy and to the Guru's grace, in the company of the sangat.
neighbors.shared: you don't have to clear the city alone.

neighbors.heading: a retreat inside
neighbors.text: Today Guru Arjan said: I remember, and remembering, remembering, I find peace. The Stoic emperor Marcus Aurelius kept a practice of turning inward too. People seek retreats, he wrote, in the country, by the sea, in the mountains, yet "it is in thy power whenever thou shalt choose to retire into thyself."
neighbors.difference: Simran turns toward the One, repeating the Name, Waheguru, again and again. Marcus turned toward his own reason and a few clear principles he kept returning to, with no Name to repeat.
neighbors.shared: peace is a place you can come back to, any time.
neighbors.sources: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations IV.3 (George Long translation)

neighbors.heading: a restless heart
neighbors.text: Today Guru Arjan said: remembering, remembering, I find peace. Saint Augustine opened his Confessions with the same discovery: "for Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee." Catholics keep remembering with short repeated prayers too, like the beads of the rosary.
neighbors.difference: In the rosary, Catholics repeat the Hail Mary, asking Mary's prayers while pondering the life of Jesus. In simran, Sikhs repeat the Name of God itself, Waheguru.
neighbors.shared: a restless heart can learn to rest, one word at a time.
neighbors.sources: Augustine, Confessions I.1 (Pusey translation, 1838) · the rosary (description)

neighbors.heading: remembered at the end
neighbors.text: Today Guru Arjan said: where no mother, father or friend can go, the Name goes with you. Hindus hear something close from Krishna in the Bhagavad Gita. In paraphrase: whoever leaves the body at the hour of death remembering me comes to my being; of this there is no doubt. So families may chant God's name beside someone dying.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, Krishna speaks as God in human form, and names himself as the one to remember. For Sikhs, the companion is the Name of the One who is never born.
neighbors.shared: there's a companion who doesn't stop at the door.

neighbors.heading: the LORD will take me up
neighbors.text: Today Guru Arjan said: where no mother or father can go, the Name goes with you. A psalm says it plainly: "For though my father and my mother have forsaken me, The LORD will take me up." And in the darkest valley: "I will fear no evil, For Thou art with me."
neighbors.difference: Psalm 23 pictures God as a shepherd, guarding a person through the darkest valley. Sukhmani follows the soul past death itself, to the meeting with death's messenger, with the Name alongside.
neighbors.shared: in the room no one else can enter, you're not alone.

neighbors.heading: where are the nine?
neighbors.text: Today Sukhmani walked through a life, milk in infancy, food in youth, family in old age, and asked how anyone forgets the Giver. Jesus once healed ten men, and only one came back to say thank you: "Were there not ten cleansed? but where are the nine?" And James wrote: "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above."
neighbors.difference: Christians give thanks above all for Jesus, whom they see as God's greatest gift; the Eucharist itself means thanksgiving. Sukhmani counts the Giver's gifts in ordinary things: milk, water, a breeze, laughter.
neighbors.shared: the ordinary things are gifts too.

neighbors.heading: too many to count
neighbors.text: Today Sukhmani listed everyday gifts, water, a breeze, hands and eyes, and asked how the Giver is forgotten. The Qur'an counts gifts too: "And if ye would count the favour of Allah ye cannot reckon it." And it promises: "If ye give thanks, I will give you more." Many Muslims say alhamdulillah, praise be to God, over the smallest things.
neighbors.difference: Islamic thanks takes set forms too, like the Fatiha, recited in every prayer, which begins al-hamdu lillah. Sikhs thank the Giver by remembering the Name and by sharing, vand chhakna, in the langar.
neighbors.shared: too many gifts to count, and still worth counting.

neighbors.heading: these thy gifts
neighbors.text: Today Guru Arjan said: by whose grace you eat fine food, keep that Master in mind. Many Catholic families say a grace before meals: "Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts, which we are about to receive from thy bounty, through Christ our Lord. Amen." The meal becomes a reminder of the Giver.
neighbors.difference: Catholics ask God to bless the food and the people at the table, through Christ. In this verse, Guru Arjan doesn't ask a blessing on the meal; he turns each comfort into remembering the One who gave it.
neighbors.shared: every meal can start with a thank you.

neighbors.heading: a pause before eating
neighbors.text: Today Guru Arjan turned each meal into a reminder of the Giver. Buddhist monks and nuns reflect before eating too. In paraphrase: reflecting wisely, I use this food not for fun, pride or beauty, but only to keep this body going, to ease hunger and support the holy life. Some lay Buddhists also pause to remember everyone whose work made the meal.
neighbors.difference: Buddhists don't thank a creator for the meal; they reflect on its purpose and honor the people who gave it. Sikhs remember the One by whose grace all food comes.
neighbors.shared: pause before you eat; something was given.
neighbors.sources: Majjhima Nikaya 2, the reflection on food (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: walk with the wise
neighbors.text: Today Sukhmani said: in the company of the holy, the face grows bright. Jews have a proverb for that rubbing-off: "He that walketh with wise men shall be wise; But the companion of fools shall smart for it." And the first psalm blesses the one who hasn't sat in the seat of the scornful.
neighbors.difference: In Jewish life, good company often gathers around Torah study, and the Mishnah says to find yourself a teacher and acquire a friend. Sikhs gather in sangat around kirtan, singing the Guru's hymns.
neighbors.shared: the people you sit with shape the person you become.

neighbors.heading: it rubs off
neighbors.text: Today Sukhmani said that in good company the face grows bright and the grime washes off. The Stoic Seneca gave a friend the same advice: "Associate with those who will make a better man of you. Welcome those whom you yourself can improve. The process is mutual; for men learn while they teach."
neighbors.difference: For Seneca, good company trains character and reason. Sukhmani's holy company gathers around the Name, and the brightness it gives is, in Sikh teaching, God's grace.
neighbors.shared: choose your company the way you'd choose good food.
neighbors.sources: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 7.8 (Gummere translation)

neighbors.heading: say what you do
neighbors.text: Today Sukhmani said the true pandit teaches his own mind first, then teaches everyone. The Qur'an asks the same of anyone who speaks: "O ye who believe! Why say ye that which ye do not? It is most hateful in the sight of Allah that ye say that which ye do not." And a hadith calls the strong one the person who masters himself in anger.
neighbors.difference: Islamic learning centers on the Qur'an, revealed to the Prophet Muhammad, and the example he lived. Sukhmani's pandit reads the old scriptures for their root and finds the Name within.
neighbors.shared: the first student a teacher has is their own mind.

neighbors.heading: the equal eye
neighbors.text: Today Sukhmani said the true pandit instructs his own mind and teaches all four castes. The Bhagavad Gita has its own picture of a true pandit. In paraphrase: the wise see with an equal eye a learned brahmin, a cow, an elephant, a dog and an outcast. In the Gita, real learning shows in how you see everyone.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, Krishna teaches as God in human form, and equal vision comes from seeing the one Self in all. Sukhmani's pandit finds the Name within, then teaches all four castes.
neighbors.shared: real learning shows in how you treat everyone.

neighbors.heading: forsake pride
neighbors.text: Today the salok said the meek one dwells in peace, having set the self down low. The Dhammapada points the same way: "Let a man leave anger, let him forsake pride, let him overcome all bondage! No sufferings befall the man who is not attached to name and form, and who calls nothing his own."
neighbors.difference: Buddhists see pride as a fetter that loosens as you see there's no fixed self to defend. Sikhs set the ego, haumai, down before the One, and humility opens the way to the Name.
neighbors.shared: the one who doesn't have to win can finally rest.

neighbors.heading: rest for your souls
neighbors.text: Today the salok said: the meek one dwells in peace. Jesus made a promise like it: "learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls." And on a hillside he said: "Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth."
neighbors.difference: For Christians, humility has a face: Jesus, whom they believe is God's Son, made lowly. In the salok, humility is setting your own self down before the One, with Nanak himself as the humble voice.
neighbors.shared: the one who doesn't have to win can finally rest.

neighbors.heading: the sea sits lowest
neighbors.text: Today Guru Arjan said: whoever knows himself low is counted highest of all. The Tao Te Ching pictures it with water: "That whereby the rivers and seas are able to receive the homage and tribute of all the valley streams, is their skill in being lower than they." The sea is great because it sits lowest.
neighbors.difference: Lao Tzu's lowness is the way of the Tao, how things naturally work, with no personal God keeping the count. Guru Arjan says it's God's own reckoning that turns the ladder over.
neighbors.shared: there's quiet strength in taking the lower seat.

neighbors.heading: the humble lifted
neighbors.text: Today Guru Arjan turned the ladder over: whoever knows himself low is counted highest. Mary sings the same reversal in the Magnificat, which the Church prays each evening: "He hath put down the mighty from their seat, and hath exalted the humble." And Jesus said: "he that humbleth himself shall be exalted."
neighbors.difference: Catholics see the reversal lived in Mary, a humble girl God chose, honored as Queen of Heaven. Sikhs remember Guru Amar Das, who served humbly for years before he became Guru.
neighbors.shared: the ladder looks different from where God stands.

neighbors.heading: when every hand fails
neighbors.text: Today Sukhmani said every human prop gives way; the Giver is the One alone. Hindus tell of Draupadi, dragged into a royal hall while the elders sat silent. In the story as it's often told, when every human help failed, she called on Krishna, and her sari never ran out. In the Gita, Krishna says, in paraphrase: take refuge in me alone.
neighbors.difference: In the story, Krishna is God come in human form, a friend at Draupadi's side. Sikhs lean on the One who is never born, met through the Name and the Guru's Word.
neighbors.shared: when every hand slips, there's still one to hold.
neighbors.sources: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, the dice game (paraphrase of the telling) · Bhagavad Gita 18:66 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: not in princes
neighbors.text: Today Sukhmani said leaning all your hope on people is in vain; the Giver is the One. A psalm says it just as plainly: "Put not your trust in princes, Nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help." And it goes on: happy is the one whose help is the God of Jacob.
neighbors.difference: The psalm's God is the God of Jacob, bound to Israel by covenant, who keeps faith forever. Sukhmani speaks of the One Giver of all, found through the Guru and the Name.
neighbors.shared: people are precious, and they can't be everything.

items.lessonTitle: Ashtpadi 16, salok: no form, no color

neighbors.heading: invisible
neighbors.text: Today Sukhmani said the One has no form, no outline, no color. Christians also speak of a God no eye can picture: "God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth." And Paul praised "the King eternal, immortal, invisible."
neighbors.difference: Christians believe the invisible God took a human face in Jesus: "he that hath seen me hath seen the Father." Sikhs hold that the formless One never takes a body, yet is present in every form.
neighbors.shared: God is more than any picture we can draw.

neighbors.heading: nothing like Him
neighbors.text: Today Sukhmani said the One has no form, no outline, no color at all. The Qur'an says it in its own words: "Naught is as His likeness; and He is the Hearer, the Seer." And a short surah ends: "And there is none comparable unto Him." So Muslims make no pictures of God.
neighbors.difference: Islam keeps God wholly distinct from creation: nothing is like Him. Sukhmani adds that the formless One is also present in every form, the light whose color everything is.
neighbors.shared: God is more than any picture we can draw.

neighbors.heading: treasure in heaven
neighbors.text: Today the salok said nothing goes along with you but devotion; the rest is ash. Paul wrote the same to Timothy: "For we brought nothing into this world: and certainly we can carry nothing out." And Jesus said: "lay up to yourselves treasures in heaven: where neither the rust nor moth doth consume."
neighbors.difference: Catholics speak of one earthly life, then judgment, with treasure stored by love of God and neighbor, through Christ. Sikh teaching speaks of the Name earned over a life, and of release from the round of births.
neighbors.shared: the things that last are the ones you can't hold.

neighbors.heading: not even yourself
neighbors.text: Today the salok said that without devotion nothing goes along with you; the rest is ash. The Dhammapada puts it sharply: "'These sons belong to me, and this wealth belongs to me,' with such thoughts a fool is tormented. He himself does not belong to himself; how much less sons and wealth?"
neighbors.difference: For Buddhists, what carries on is karma, the shape of one's actions, and the deeper aim is letting go of "mine" altogether. The salok says to earn a different wealth: the Name of the Lord.
neighbors.shared: hold your things lightly; they were never fully yours.

neighbors.heading: only good deeds
neighbors.text: Today Sukhmani said the Name of the Lord is the wealth that travels with you. The rabbis said something close. In paraphrase: when a person departs, neither silver nor gold nor jewels go along, only Torah and good deeds. And a proverb says: "Treasures of wickedness profit nothing; But righteousness delivereth from death."
neighbors.difference: In the rabbis' saying, what goes along is Torah, God's teaching to Israel, studied and lived. For Sikhs, it's the Name of the One, remembered and earned, alongside the kindness you've shared.
neighbors.shared: kindness done is something you get to keep.

neighbors.heading: giving as keeping
neighbors.text: Today Sukhmani said the wealth that goes along is the Lord's Name, gathered by remembering. The Tao Te Ching says giving is a strange kind of keeping: "The sage does not accumulate (for himself). The more that he expends for others, the more does he possess (of his own)."
neighbors.difference: Lao Tzu speaks of this life and the way of the Tao, not of what travels after death. Sukhmani speaks of the soul's long road, and of the Name of the Lord as its truest wealth.
neighbors.shared: what you give away is somehow still yours.

neighbors.heading: nearer than a heartbeat
neighbors.text: Today Sukhmani said the One lives in every heart, ghat ghat, every clay jar. Muslims hear God's nearness in the Qur'an's own words: "We are nearer to him than his jugular vein." The verse says God already knows what a person's soul whispers to itself, before a word is spoken.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the One's Light shines within every being. For Muslims, God is closer than anything, yet never dwells inside creation; He is near in knowing and care, and wholly other than what He made.
neighbors.shared: no one is ever as far from God as they feel.

neighbors.heading: the lord in the heart
neighbors.text: Today Sukhmani said God dwells in every heart, and so the langar seats everyone in the same rows. Hindus hear something close in the Bhagavad Gita. Near its end, Krishna tells Arjuna that the Lord dwells in the heart of all beings, turning them as if on a wheel by His power.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs speak of the One Light in every heart, the One who is never born and takes no incarnation. In the Gita it is Krishna, honored by many Hindus as God come in human form, who speaks of the Lord in the heart.
neighbors.shared: the stranger beside you carries the same light you do.

items.lessonTitle: Ashtpadi 23, salok: the ointment of wisdom

neighbors.heading: the eye arose
neighbors.text: Today the Guru's wisdom was an ointment for the eyes, and the darkness simply ended. Buddhists remember the Buddha's first teaching in a deer park. Describing his awakening, he says that about things never heard before, vision arose, knowledge, wisdom and true knowledge arose, and light arose.
neighbors.difference: In the salok, the Guru applies the ointment by God's grace. In the Buddha's teaching, the light comes through seeing the way things are for oneself, with no creator to grant it, though a teacher points the way.
neighbors.shared: the world was there all along; clear eyes let you see it.

neighbors.heading: now i see
neighbors.text: Today the Guru cleared the seeker's eyes, and the dark room filled with light. Christians remember a man born blind whom Jesus healed with clay on his eyes. Pressed with questions about who had healed him, he answered simply: "one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see."
neighbors.difference: In the salok, the ointment is the Guru's wisdom, clearing inner sight. In the Gospel, the healing is told as a real cure of a man's eyes by Jesus, whom Christians follow as the light of the world.
neighbors.shared: sometimes all you can say is, i see now.

neighbors.heading: out of the cave
neighbors.text: Today Guru Angad said a hundred moons and a thousand suns still leave us dark without the Guru. Plato told a story of people chained in a cave, taking shadows on the wall for the whole world. Someone has to turn one of them around and lead them, squinting, up into the sun.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the light is the Guru, the Word teaching from within, carried by the Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib. For Plato, the light is the Good, reached by reason, and any guide out of the cave is a fellow human.
neighbors.shared: plenty of light outside doesn't mean you can see.
neighbors.sources: Plato, Republic, Book VII, the allegory of the cave (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the light of life
neighbors.text: Today Guru Angad said the brightest sky can't reach the darkness the Guru lifts. Catholics hear Jesus in the Gospel: "I am the light of the world: he that followeth me, walketh not in darkness, but shall have the light of life." At the Easter Vigil, a single candle is carried into a dark church.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the light is the Guru's Word, now the Guru Granth Sahib. For Catholics, the light is a person, Jesus Christ, God made man, met in the Church and the sacraments.
neighbors.shared: the light that matters most shows you which way to turn.

neighbors.heading: the wind keeps its place
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak sang that in awe the wind blows, the rivers run, and the sun keeps its course. Hindus have an old echo. The Taittiriya Upanishad says that from awe of the Supreme the wind blows and the sun rises, and fire, Indra and Death all go about their work.
neighbors.difference: In the Upanishad, the Supreme is Brahman, the ground of all, and the gods are honored powers within its order. In the salok, only the Formless is without fear; gods and heroes stand in awe with everyone else.
neighbors.shared: everything keeps faith with its place in a larger order.

neighbors.heading: fulfilling his word
neighbors.text: Today the salok said wind, rivers and fire all move in awe of the One. A psalm calls the whole of creation to praise, the sun and moon, the deep seas, and "stormy wind, fulfilling His word." Jews name the right response yirat shamayim, the awe of heaven, which keeps a life upright.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs hear the wind moving within hukam, the One's order. In the psalm, creation obeys the word of the God who made it, and for Jews, human awe takes shape in keeping the Torah.
neighbors.shared: awe is knowing where you belong, not being afraid.

neighbors.heading: lowliness of mind
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak called sweetness and humility the essence of every virtue: the side that bends low is the heavy one. Christians hear Paul writing to a church in Philippi: "in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves." He points to Jesus, who he says took the form of a servant.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, humility grows by remembering the Name and losing ego. For Christians, the pattern is Jesus himself, believed to be God who humbled himself to become human and die on a cross.
neighbors.shared: the one who bends low is often the one who holds the most.

neighbors.heading: walking gently
neighbors.text: Today the salok named two words, sweetness and humility, and called them the heart of goodness. The Qur'an draws a portrait of the faithful: they "walk upon the earth modestly, and when the foolish ones address them answer: Peace." Low in step, sweet in reply.
neighbors.difference: In the salok, humility is the weight on the scale that shows real value. In the Qur'an, it's a mark of servants of the Merciful, whose whole life is surrender to Allah.
neighbors.shared: a gentle answer can end a fight before it starts.

neighbors.heading: the bond of perfection
neighbors.text: Today young Nanak asked for a thread spun from compassion, contentment, restraint and truth. Saint Paul tells Christians to put on mercy, kindness, humility and patience like clothing, and then ties them all together: "above all these things have charity, which is the bond of perfection." Love is what holds the rest.
neighbors.difference: In the salok, compassion is the raw cotton everything else is spun from. For Catholics, charity is love poured into the heart by God, received in baptism, and it binds the other virtues.
neighbors.shared: goodness needs one strong strand to hold it together.

neighbors.heading: not by birth
neighbors.text: Today the salok asked what makes a sacred thread holy, and answered with compassion and truth. Buddhists remember the Buddha asking a similar question about the priestly class of his day. In the Dhammapada he says no one is a brahmin by birth, family or matted hair, but by truth and goodness.
neighbors.difference: Nanak spins his virtues into a thread of the soul for God. The Buddha's verse is about a person's conduct leading toward freedom from suffering, with no creator in view.
neighbors.shared: what's inside a person counts more than what they wear.

neighbors.heading: i will wake the dawn
neighbors.text: Today the Asa di Var was sung in the hours around sunrise, in amrit vela. A psalm wants to beat the sun up: "awake, psaltery and harp; I will awake the dawn." Many Jews pray Shacharit, the morning service, every day, and the Talmud praises those who time their prayer to the sunrise.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs sing the Guru's hymns with the ragis, often over hours. Jewish morning prayer is a fixed order of blessings, psalms and the Shema, said in Hebrew, ideally with a minyan of ten.
neighbors.shared: the first hour of the day can belong to something bigger.

neighbors.heading: a cheerful invitation
neighbors.text: Today the var was sung while the sky went from black to gray to gold. Thoreau, living by a pond, wrote of the morning too: "Every morning was a cheerful invitation to make my life of equal simplicity, and I may say innocence, with Nature herself." He rose early and bathed in the pond.
neighbors.difference: In amrit vela, Sikhs rise to remember the true Name and sing the Guru's words. Thoreau met the dawn as a fresh start, with nature as his teacher, not a fixed prayer.
neighbors.shared: before the noise starts, the day is still yours to shape.
neighbors.sources: Henry David Thoreau, Walden, "Where I Lived, and What I Lived For" (1854)

neighbors.heading: an atom's weight
neighbors.text: Today the Katak stanza said we earn what our deeds earn, and no one else is to blame. The Qur'an puts it in the smallest unit it can: "whoso doeth good an atom's weight will see it then, and whoso doeth ill an atom's weight will see it then." Nothing done is lost.
neighbors.difference: Sikh teaching holds deeds and the Guru's grace together, across the round of births. In Islam, every deed is weighed on one Day of Judgment, before a just and merciful God, after one life.
neighbors.shared: owning what you did is where every repair begins.

neighbors.heading: as you act
neighbors.text: Today Guru Arjan's Katak stanza said we reap what we did, so blame no one. Hindus call that law karma. An old Upanishad says that as a person acts, so they become: doing good, they become good; doing harm, they become harmful. Desire shapes will, will shapes deeds, and deeds shape who we are.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs and Hindus share the word karma. In the Sikh stanza, the deepest deed is forgetting the Lord, and the Guru's mercy can still reach the field. Hindu schools describe release in their own ways: knowledge, devotion or selfless action.
neighbors.shared: the field you stand in is the one you planted.

items.lessonTitle: The world as a wall of sand

neighbors.heading: like a dream
neighbors.text: Today the ninth Guru said this creation passes like a dream in the night, or a cloud's shadow on a field. A well-known Buddhist verse closes the Diamond Sutra the same way: see everything made like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, dew, a flash of lightning. Look at it that way, it says.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the passing world is still the Lord's creation, and the steady thing is His shelter. Buddhists see impermanence as the nature of everything conditioned, with no creator behind them, and seeing it clearly loosens suffering.
neighbors.shared: hold what you love gently; it was never yours to grip.

neighbors.heading: a vapour
neighbors.text: Today the Guru called the body a dream that comes in the night. Christians hear James, who warned people making big plans for next year: "For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away." Instead, he says, add "if the Lord will."
neighbors.difference: The Guru points to the Lord's shelter and the Name as what lasts. For Christians, what lasts is life with God through Christ, and they hope for the resurrection of the body, not only release from it.
neighbors.shared: plans are good; holding them lightly is better.

neighbors.heading: not the thing, the opinion
neighbors.text: Today the ninth Guru drew a portrait of someone who, in pain, doesn't crown pain king. The Stoic teacher Epictetus, once a slave, taught nearly the same steadiness: "Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things." Our judgments, he said, are ours to work on.
neighbors.difference: For the Guru, the steady one has merged with the Lord, like water into water. For Epictetus, steadiness comes from reason, sorting what is in our power from what isn't.
neighbors.shared: you can feel the storm without letting it steer.

neighbors.heading: health or sickness
neighbors.text: Today the hymn praised the one who sees gold and dust alike, unmoved by praise or blame. Saint Ignatius of Loyola asks the same of people making his Spiritual Exercises: be free inside, not preferring health to sickness, riches to poverty, honor to dishonor, a long life to a short one, for the sake of God.
neighbors.difference: The Guru describes one who has merged with the Lord. Ignatius calls this freedom indifference: choosing whatever best serves the purpose he names, to praise, reverence and serve God, and so be saved.
neighbors.shared: freedom inside lets you choose well when life shifts.
neighbors.sources: Ignatius of Loyola, Spiritual Exercises, Principle and Foundation (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: no one shrinks from them
neighbors.text: Today the ninth Guru called someone wise who frightens no one and fears no one. Hindus hear a close match in the Gita. Krishna names who is dear to him: the one from whom the world doesn't shrink, and who doesn't shrink from the world, free of joy, envy, fear and agitation.
neighbors.difference: In the salok, the fearless one begins to resemble the One who is nirbhau and nirvair, without fear or enmity. In the Gita, it's a mark of the devotee whom Krishna, God for many Hindus, holds dear.
neighbors.shared: courage and gentleness can live in the same person.

neighbors.heading: whom shall i fear
neighbors.text: Today the salok asked for a person who gives fear to no one and takes it from no one. The Torah pairs two ideas in one verse: "ye shall not wrong one another; but thou shalt fear thy God." And a psalm finishes the thought: "The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?"
neighbors.difference: Sikhs aim to become fearless, like the Formless. In Judaism, fear of God, reverent awe, stays at the center of a life, and the psalm finds in God freedom from every other fear.
neighbors.shared: a heart steady in the right place frightens no one.

neighbors.heading: call on the name
neighbors.text: Today the Name was a boat across a stormy ocean. Christians often call on a name too. Paul writes: "For whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved." The Gospels tell of Jesus asleep in a boat in a storm, woken by frightened friends, and the sea going calm.
neighbors.difference: In Sikh teaching the boat is Naam, remembering the formless One. For Christians the name is Jesus, believed to be the Son of God, and being saved means life with God through his death and rising.
neighbors.shared: in the worried hour, you don't have to swim alone.

neighbors.heading: in the name of allah
neighbors.text: Today the ninth Guru said the Name carries a person across the terrifying sea. The Qur'an tells of Noah loading the ark as the flood began. He told those with him: "Embark therein! In the name of Allah be its course and its mooring." Muslims begin a journey, a meal, almost anything, with bismillah, in the name of Allah.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the boat is simran, remembering the Name across the round of births. In Islam, saying Allah's name is a believer's trust in one God, whose mercy is hoped for on the Last Day.
neighbors.shared: a name said in trust can carry you through the waves.

neighbors.heading: unto dust
neighbors.text: Today the salok said whatever is born will pass, today or tomorrow, so sing. Catholics hear it on Ash Wednesday, when ashes are pressed on foreheads with words from Genesis: "for dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return." Then comes Lent, forty days to turn back toward God.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the passing is hukam, and the Name is what stays. Catholics believe the dust is not the end: they hope for the resurrection of the body, through Christ's own rising at Easter.
neighbors.shared: knowing life is short is a reason to spend it well.

neighbors.heading: the last words
neighbors.text: Today the ninth Guru said whatever has sprung up will perish, and the date is the only open question. Buddhists remember the Buddha's last words, spoken as he lay dying: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" Passing, and so, effort.
neighbors.difference: The Guru answers passing with praise of the Lord and the Name. The Buddha answers it with diligent practice, walking the path to the end of suffering, with no creator in view.
neighbors.shared: the frost is coming; pick the tomatoes and share them.

neighbors.heading: he laid his hands
neighbors.text: Today the Ardas remembered Guru Nanak handing the Guruship to his disciple Lehna, by fitness, not by blood. Jews remember Moses and his student Joshua: "Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom; for Moses had laid his hands upon him." The Mishnah traces the chain: Moses received the Torah and handed it to Joshua.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the same light passed from Nanak to Angad, and later to the Guru Granth Sahib. In Judaism, Moses stays unique among prophets; what passes on is the Torah and its teaching, not Moses himself.
neighbors.shared: a good teacher is measured by who carries it next.

neighbors.heading: from my grandfather
neighbors.text: Today the Ardas named the Gurus one by one, a teacher, then a student who became a teacher. The emperor Marcus Aurelius began his private notebook the same way: a list of those who formed him. From his grandfather, good morals; from his mother, a simple way of living; from teacher after teacher, what each gave.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs remember the Gurus as one divine light in ten bodies. Marcus thanks ordinary people for ordinary gifts, and the gods for the good fortune of having known them.
neighbors.shared: you're made of everyone who took the time to teach you.

neighbors.heading: forgive and overlook
neighbors.text: Today the Ardas honored those who saw others' faults and chose to make them unseen. The Qur'an asks the same of people with a real grievance: "Let them forgive and show indulgence. Yearn ye not that Allah may forgive you?" A hadith adds that whoever covers a brother's fault, Allah will cover theirs.
neighbors.difference: In the Ardas, overlooking sits beside the sword: let the slight go, but stand against cruelty. In the Qur'an, forgiving is mercy from people who hope for Allah's mercy, and justice against wrong is upheld too.
neighbors.shared: some of the best things people do are invisible on purpose.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 24:22 (Pickthall 1930) · Sahih Muslim, on covering faults (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: no fault-finding
neighbors.text: Today the Ardas remembered people who saw clearly, and let it go. Hindus find the same habit in the Gita's list of divine qualities: gentleness, forgiveness, compassion toward all beings, and an aversion to finding fault. Krishna counts it among the marks of someone born with a divine nature.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs ask God's help to live as those Ardas heroes did, in a community that also protects. In the Gita, these qualities are part of a person's nature and dharma, leading toward freedom.
neighbors.shared: a family runs on people who decide not to keep score.

neighbors.heading: faith is the seed
neighbors.text: Today the Ardas asked for trust and faith as gifts. Buddhists talk about faith too, saddha, confidence in the Buddha's way. A farmer once mocked the Buddha for not plowing, and the Buddha answered that he did plow: faith is his seed, discipline the rain, wisdom his yoke and plow.
neighbors.difference: In the Ardas, faith is a gift asked of God. In the early Buddhist texts, faith is confidence a person tests and grows by practice, with no God who grants it.
neighbors.shared: trust grows best when you keep tending it.

neighbors.heading: the gift of god
neighbors.text: Today the Ardas asked for faith as daan, a gift freely given, not earned. Many Christians speak of faith that way. Paul writes: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God." Many Christians pray for more of it, like the father in the Gospel: help my unbelief.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs ask for faith alongside discipline, uncut hair and discernment, the gifts of a Sikh life. For Christians, faith is trust in Jesus Christ, and grace through him is the gift that saves.
neighbors.shared: faith can be something you ask for, not only something you have.

neighbors.heading: the swarm and the bee
neighbors.text: Today the Ardas widened at its end: by Your will, good for all. Marcus Aurelius, writing in his private notebook, kept coming back to the same idea, that we are made for one another. One line says it in a single picture: "That which is not good for the swarm, neither is it good for the bee."
neighbors.difference: The Ardas asks good for all of God, by His will. Marcus reasons it out: a person is part of one human community, so his own good can't be separated from everyone's.
neighbors.shared: your good and everyone's good are tied together.

neighbors.heading: for all men
neighbors.text: Today the Ardas ended with good for all, no one left off the list. Catholics pray that wide at Mass, in the prayers of the faithful, following Saint Paul: "I desire therefore, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all men." Rulers, strangers, enemies, the whole world.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs close with chardi kala, rising spirits through the Name, and ask good for all in God's will. Catholics pray through Christ, whom they believe gave himself for all people.
neighbors.shared: a prayer can end by widening to include everyone.

neighbors.heading: offered first
neighbors.text: Today Sikhs paused before food to thank the Giver. Some Hindu families say a Gita verse before eating: the offering is Brahman, the food is Brahman, offered by Brahman into the fire of Brahman. In temples and homes, food is often offered to God first, then shared as prasad, a blessing.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs say Ardas over food, in the gurdwara before the Guru Granth Sahib, with no image or idol. Hindus often offer food before a sacred image, a murti, where many feel God is present to receive it.
neighbors.shared: a meal given thanks for is hard to eat in a rush.

neighbors.heading: bless after you eat
neighbors.text: Today the Ardas made a pause before the plate. Jews bless God before eating: over bread, for bringing forth bread from the earth. And the Torah adds a blessing after: "thou shalt eat and be satisfied, and bless the LORD thy God for the good land which He hath given thee."
neighbors.difference: Sikhs pray an Ardas, in their own words or a few set lines, before the meal. Jewish blessings are fixed words, said before each kind of food, and the longest grace comes after the meal, once you're full.
neighbors.shared: food is a gift, so the table starts with thanks.
neighbors.sources: Deuteronomy 8:10 (JPS 1917) · the blessing over bread, hamotzi (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the whole world
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak imagined a palace of pearls and prayed only not to forget. Jesus asked a question his followers still carry: "For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?" He also told of a rich man who built bigger barns and forgot what mattered.
neighbors.difference: Guru Nanak doesn't ask for less, only to remember the Giver. Jesus also called some followers to leave everything and follow him, and Christians honor both householders and those who give it all away.
neighbors.shared: a beautiful life can still make you forget the one who gave it.

neighbors.heading: let it not distract
neighbors.text: Today the shabad asked that no palace or throne make the Name slip from mind. The Qur'an gives the same warning to believers: "Let not your wealth nor your children distract you from remembrance of Allah." It doesn't call wealth or children bad. It names the danger as forgetting.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, remembering is simran of the Name, all through the day. Muslims keep that remembrance, dhikr, with phrases like subhan Allah, and five set prayers a day turn them back to Allah.
neighbors.shared: good things are safest when you remember where they came from.

neighbors.heading: one father
neighbors.text: Today Guru Arjan sang: one Father, and we are all His children. The prophet Malachi asked his people almost the same question: "Have we not all one father? hath not one God created us?" And then the sharp part: why then does each of us despise his brother? Catholics see every person as made in God's image.
neighbors.difference: Guru Arjan's Father is the formless One, with no incarnation. Catholics know God as Father through Jesus, his Son, and speak of becoming God's adopted children through baptism.
neighbors.shared: the person you like least still sits at the same family table.
neighbors.sources: Malachi 2:10 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1265 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: as a mother
neighbors.text: Today the shabad said we all belong to each other, with no one voted off. Buddhists reach the same circle with a different picture. The Metta Sutta asks: as a mother would guard her only child with her life, so let one keep a boundless heart toward all beings, above, below and across.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, we are siblings because we share one Father. Buddhism speaks of no creator; the kinship comes from a heart of loving-kindness that a person grows until it leaves no one out.
neighbors.shared: nobody has to earn a place in the family.

neighbors.heading: one flesh
neighbors.text: Today the fourth round closed the wedding, and Sikhs remembered: one light in two bodies. Jews read their own picture in Genesis: a man "shall cleave unto his wife, and they shall be one flesh." At many Jewish weddings the bride circles the groom under the chuppah, and seven blessings are sung.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs read the laavan on two levels, a marriage and a soul's journey to God, sealed by circling the Guru Granth Sahib. A Jewish marriage is a covenant between two people, made with a ring and a written ketubah.
neighbors.shared: a wedding is a walk you start together and keep walking.

neighbors.heading: spaces in your togetherness
neighbors.text: Today the fourth round ended in sahaj, the ease of two lives at rest together. Kahlil Gibran, writing about marriage in The Prophet, adds a gentle balance: "let there be spaces in your togetherness." Two pillars hold up one temple, he says, standing apart.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the couple becomes one light in two bodies, and the union points toward God. Gibran prizes the closeness and also the space, so each stays whole.
neighbors.shared: love can be one light and still leave room to breathe.

neighbors.heading: the most beautiful names
neighbors.text: Today Guru Arjan sang Ram and Khuda, Kareem and Raheem, in one shabad. The Qur'an has its own word on names: "Cry unto Allah, or cry unto the Beneficent, unto whichsoever ye cry (it is the same). His are the most beautiful names." Muslims learn many of them: the Merciful, the Generous, the Peace.
neighbors.difference: Guru Arjan's shabad sees Hindu and Muslim names pointing to one Lord. The Qur'an's verse is about the names Allah gives Himself; in Islam, God's names are learned from revelation.
neighbors.shared: the name you call on matters, and so does the one you're calling.

neighbors.heading: the wise call it many
neighbors.text: Today the shabad walked down a street where neighbors call God Ram, Khuda, Gusain, Allah. Hindus have an old line from the Rig Veda often quoted for the same spirit: truth is one, and the wise call it by many names. The hymn lists the names the poets of its day used.
neighbors.difference: Guru Arjan says what counts is recognizing the one Lord's hukam. Many Hindus honor that one truth through many forms and images of God, which Sikhs do not worship.
neighbors.shared: a neighbor's prayer deserves your respect, even in other words.

neighbors.heading: chanted at the bedside
neighbors.text: Today a shabad sung for a sick friend was a gift. Buddhists keep that custom too. A sutta tells of the elder Mahakassapa lying ill, and the Buddha coming to recite the seven factors of awakening for him; the elder recovered. Theravada monks still chant protective verses, paritta, for the sick.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs sing the Guru's own Word and end with Ardas to God. Buddhist chanting recalls the Buddha's teaching, and its strength is in the truth and goodwill of the words, not a prayer to a creator.
neighbors.shared: when you don't know what to say, you can sing.

neighbors.heading: sing psalms
neighbors.text: Today Sikh families gathered with kirtan around someone ill. A letter in the New Testament gives Christians the same instinct: "Is any merry? let him sing psalms. Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him." Many churches still bring hymns to hospital rooms.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs offer the Guru's company through the shabad, the Guru's living voice. Christians pray in the name of Jesus, and many churches anoint the sick with oil, as the same letter describes.
neighbors.shared: a shaky voice at a bedside is still a gift.

neighbors.heading: who you eat with
neighbors.text: Today Sikhs remembered Mata Khivi, mother of the langar, feeding everyone who came. The philosopher Seneca passed on a saying of Epicurus: think first about whom you'll eat and drink with, before what. A meal without a friend, he said, is the life of a lion or a wolf.
neighbors.difference: The langar feeds strangers, anyone at all, as service to the One. Epicurus valued the table for friendship, a circle chosen with care, as part of a calm and happy life.
neighbors.shared: a shared meal feeds more than the body.

neighbors.heading: you gave me to eat
neighbors.text: Today the langar's open kitchen came from Mata Khivi at Khadur. Catholics count feeding the hungry first among the corporal works of mercy, from Jesus's own words: "For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat." In the same story, he says what's done for the least is done for him.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs serve langar to everyone as seva, seeing the One's light in every guest. Catholics feed the hungry as if feeding Christ himself, who they believe is present in the poor.
neighbors.shared: an open kitchen says, you belong here.

neighbors.heading: the joints of the day
neighbors.text: Today the daily banis framed the day: praise before dawn, Rehras at dusk, Sohila at bedtime. Some Hindus keep sandhya vandana, prayers at the meeting points of the day, dawn, noon and dusk. At its heart is the Gayatri mantra from the Rig Veda, asking the light to inspire our minds.
neighbors.difference: Sikh Nitnem is a set of the Gurus' hymns, read by anyone. Sandhya is a Vedic rite with water and mantra, traditionally kept by those given the sacred thread, while other Hindus keep their own home prayer.
neighbors.shared: a day held between prayers feels held all the way through.

neighbors.heading: lying down, rising up
neighbors.text: Today Sikhs looked back on a day framed in words, from amritvela to Kirtan Sohila. Jews frame the day too. The Shema tells them to speak God's words "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up," and many say it morning and night, with a bedtime Shema before sleep.
neighbors.difference: Sikh Nitnem is the hymns of the Gurus, in Punjabi and older tongues. Jewish prayer centers on the Shema and the Amidah, in Hebrew, three services a day.
neighbors.shared: the first and last words of a day can be the same.

neighbors.heading: hid in mine heart
neighbors.text: Today Sikhs chose one line from the year to carry. Christians have a long habit of the same thing: learning a verse by heart. A psalm says why: "Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee." Many churches still give children a memory verse to learn each week.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs take the hukamnama as the living Guru's word for the day. Christians read Scripture as God's word that points to Jesus Christ, whom they call the Word made flesh.
neighbors.shared: a line kept by heart is there at the red light.

neighbors.heading: easy to remember
neighbors.text: Today the lesson asked for one line of bani, carried and turned over for months. Muslims memorize the Qur'an, some all of it, many children a few short surahs. A verse repeats like a refrain: "And in truth We have made the Qur'an easy to remember; but is there any that remembereth?"
neighbors.difference: Sikhs treat the Guru Granth Sahib as the living Guru and read a hymn as the day's order. Muslims hold the Qur'an as Allah's own word, recited in Arabic, word for word.
neighbors.shared: words you carry inside keep opening as you grow.

neighbors.heading: God among the pots and pans
neighbors.text: Today Nanak took off the pilgrim's robe and kept his prayers inside an ordinary village day. Catholics tell of Brother Lawrence, a Carmelite who worked for years in a monastery kitchen. He said the noise and clatter of the kitchen never kept him from God; he could pray among the pots as quietly as on his knees before the altar.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, Nanak set aside the wanderer's life for the householder's, with family and farm. Brother Lawrence stayed a vowed brother in a religious house; Catholics honor both callings, the cloister and the family, as places to find God.
neighbors.shared: the holiest room you enter today may be your kitchen.
neighbors.sources: Brother Lawrence, The Practice of the Presence of God, the conversations (paraphrase) · Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Var 1, pauri 38 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: drawing water, carrying wood
neighbors.text: Today Nanak came home, put on ordinary clothes, and kept his prayers between the farming and the meals. Zen Buddhists tell of Layman Pang, a householder who never became a monk. Asked about his practice, he answered with a short verse: his wonderful powers were drawing water and carrying firewood. The awake life, in this telling, looks a lot like chores.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the householder's day is held together by remembering God's Name. In Zen, the point is waking up fully to each moment and seeing clearly; the practice doesn't rest on a Creator.
neighbors.shared: you don't need a robe to live awake.
neighbors.sources: Layman Pang's verse, in The Transmission of the Lamp (paraphrase) · Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Var 1, pauri 38 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: where ten sit together
neighbors.text: Today Bhai Gurdas counted: one is a Sikh, two a holy company, and where five gather, God is there. Jewish sages counted too. In Pirkei Avot, Rabbi Halafta teaches that when ten sit together over Torah, the Divine Presence rests among them, and then counts down: five, three, two, even one alone. Some prayers wait for a minyan, ten together.
neighbors.difference: In Bhai Gurdas's line, five is the number where God's presence is named, and later the Khalsa rests on five. In Jewish practice, a quorum of ten, the minyan, is needed for certain prayers, and the gathering in the saying centers on Torah study.
neighbors.shared: a few people around one table is already holy company.
neighbors.sources: Pirkei Avot 3:6 (paraphrase) · Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Var 13, pauri 19 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: something happens when we gather
neighbors.text: Today Bhai Gurdas said one is a Sikh, and two already make a holy company. The sociologist Émile Durkheim noticed something like it from outside any one faith. When people gather and share a rite, he wrote, a kind of electricity rises among them and lifts each person beyond themselves. He called it collective effervescence: the lift in a room where everyone sings together.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, what fills the gathering is God's presence, met in the company where the Name is sung. Durkheim explained that lift as the power of the group itself, a social fact anyone can study.
neighbors.shared: we become more than ourselves when we come together.
neighbors.sources: Émile Durkheim, The Elementary Forms of Religious Life (1912) (paraphrase) · Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Var 13, pauri 19 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: for love of Him
neighbors.text: Today Nand Lal's kitchen fed a traveler at an odd hour, no questions asked. Muslims hear the same open hand in the Qur'an, which praises those who feed the needy, the orphan and the prisoner for love of God, saying: "We feed you, for the sake of Allah only. We wish for no reward nor thanks from you."
neighbors.difference: In the Sikh story, the traveler turns out to be the Guru, so every guest is served as if he might be. In the Qur'an, the guest stays the guest; the feeding is done for God's sake, and God alone gives the reward.
neighbors.shared: a hungry person at the door is never an interruption.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 76:8–9 (Pickthall 1930) · sakhi of Bhai Nand Lal's langar at Anandpur (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the guest is God
neighbors.text: Today the Guru came to Nand Lal's kitchen dressed as a traveler, and was fed straight away. Hindus have a teaching that fits that door. In the Taittiriya Upanishad, a teacher sends his students home with a few lines to live by, among them atithi devo bhava: let the guest be as God to you. Hospitality, in that line, becomes worship.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, langar serves everyone the same food, seated side by side, whoever they are. In the Upanishad's line, the guest is honored as God by the host's household; the teaching is about the host's reverence more than a shared table.
neighbors.shared: whoever knocks might be the holiest visitor of your day.
neighbors.sources: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11.2 (paraphrase) · sakhi of Bhai Nand Lal's langar at Anandpur (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the birth stories
neighbors.text: Today we met the janamsakhis, stories of Nanak's life told to carry a teaching. Buddhists keep birth stories too: the Jatakas, tales of the Buddha's earlier lives, as a monkey, a deer, a king. Each one is told to show a good quality, like generosity or patience, growing over many lifetimes. They're told to children and grown-ups alike.
neighbors.difference: The janamsakhis tell of one life, Guru Nanak's, and Sikhs weigh them against the Guru's hymns. The Jatakas tell of many past lives, resting on the Buddhist teaching of rebirth, and their verses sit inside the Pali scriptures.
neighbors.shared: a good story can carry what a lecture can't.
neighbors.sources: the Jataka tales (paraphrase) · the janamsakhi traditions of Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: most surely believed
neighbors.text: Today we met the janamsakhis, Nanak's life written down from what was remembered and retold. Christians know that road from memory to page. Luke opens his Gospel: "Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to set forth in order a declaration of those things which are most surely believed among us." He says it came from those who were there from the beginning.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, the Gospels are scripture, the inspired word about Jesus. For Sikhs, the janamsakhis are loved stories, not scripture; the Guru's own hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib are the measure every story is weighed against.
neighbors.shared: love remembers, and then it writes things down.
neighbors.sources: Luke 1:1–2 (KJV) · the janamsakhi traditions of Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: music reaches the inward places
neighbors.text: Today Mardana forgot himself under a spell, and a song brought him back. Philosophers have wondered at that power too. In Plato's Republic, Socrates says training in music matters so much because rhythm and harmony find their way into the inmost places of the soul and take hold there. A song can reach a part of us an argument can't.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, it's the Guru's word, sung in kirtan, that breaks the spell of maya and turns a person back to God. Plato prized music for shaping character, a training of the soul toward a well-ordered life.
neighbors.shared: sometimes a song remembers who you are before you do.
neighbors.sources: Plato, Republic, book 3, 401d (paraphrase) · Janamsakhi tradition, the bewitching of Mardana (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: weeping at the hymns
neighbors.text: Today a hymn broke a spell and brought Mardana back to himself. Saint Augustine tells of something like it in his Confessions. In the church at Milan, he writes, the hymns and the voices of the people flowed into his ears, truth seeped into his heart, and tears ran down, and he was glad of them. The singing helped bring a restless man home.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, kirtan is the Guru's own word, sung, and singing it is a central way of remembering God. For Catholics, hymns serve the liturgy, whose heart is the Mass; Augustine was moved by Christ's Church singing together.
neighbors.shared: a song can find you when you've lost your way.
neighbors.sources: Augustine, Confessions 9.6 (paraphrase) · Janamsakhi tradition, the bewitching of Mardana (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: The boy who feared the fire

neighbors.heading: a boy who asked death
neighbors.text: Today a cowherd boy noticed that the small sticks catch fire first, and came to sit with Nanak. Hindus tell of another young one who wouldn't put off the big question. In the Katha Upanishad, the boy Nachiketa goes to Yama, the lord of death, and is offered riches and long life instead of an answer. He turns them down, and asks what lies beyond.
neighbors.difference: Nachiketa is taught about the Self that is never born and never dies. The cowherd boy, later called Baba Buddha, found his answer in a lifetime of serving the Gurus and remembering God's Name.
neighbors.shared: a young person's big question deserves a real answer.
neighbors.sources: Katha Upanishad 1.1–1.2 (paraphrase) · sakhi of Bhai Bura and the kindling (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: one day before you die
neighbors.text: Today a boy saw that death takes the young too. Rabbi Eliezer taught: turn back to God one day before your death. His students asked how anyone knows that day. Exactly, he said: so turn back today, and your whole life is spent turning. A psalm prays: "So teach us to number our days, that we may get us a heart of wisdom."
neighbors.difference: The boy, later called Baba Buddha, came to sit with the Guru and remember God's Name. For Jews, the turning is teshuvah, coming back to God and the Torah's commandments, renewed each day and above all on Yom Kippur.
neighbors.shared: today is a good day to begin.
neighbors.sources: Pirkei Avot 2:10 (2:15 in some editions) and Talmud Shabbat 153a (paraphrase) · Psalm 90:12 (JPS 1917) · sakhi of Bhai Bura and the kindling (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: four Gospels, one story
neighbors.text: Today we saw sakhis tell the same story in different places, while the lesson stays put. Christians read four Gospels side by side. Matthew, Mark, Luke and John each tell of Jesus feeding a hungry crowd, with details that don't all match. Augustine wrote a whole book, The Harmony of the Gospels, taking each telling seriously and showing how they fit.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, all four Gospels are scripture, each inspired in its own voice. For Sikhs, the janamsakhis are not scripture; the Guru Granth Sahib holds the highest authority, so the stories can differ without the ground moving.
neighbors.shared: a story told by many voices can still be true.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 14, Mark 6, Luke 9, John 6 (paraphrase) · Augustine, The Harmony of the Gospels (paraphrase) · janamsakhi traditions (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: weighing the reports
neighbors.text: Today we saw that comparing sakhis can be a kind of care. Muslims have a long science of that care. The sayings of the Prophet Muhammad, the hadith, came down through chains of narrators, and scholars like al-Bukhari sifted the reports, weighing who heard what from whom. Above every report stands the Qur'an, which Muslims hold as God's own word.
neighbors.difference: Hadith scholars judge each report largely by its chain of trustworthy narrators, and sound hadith carry deep authority in Muslim law and life. For Sikhs, the sakhis are loved and taught, but the hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib decide.
neighbors.shared: careful questions are a way of loving what's handed down.
neighbors.sources: Sahih al-Bukhari and the science of hadith (paraphrase) · janamsakhi traditions (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: now not I
neighbors.text: Today Kabir sang of a dying that brings joy: the ego letting go while life goes on. Catholics hear that in Saint Paul: "With Christ I am nailed to the cross. And I live, now not I; but Christ liveth in me." Catholic saints speak of dying to self, so a new life can grow in the same body, at the same kitchen sink.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, dying to self happens in Christ: in baptism a person shares his death and rising, and grace makes the new life. For Sikhs, the ego, haumai, loosens through the Guru's word and the Name, and freedom can be lived now.
neighbors.shared: the grip can loosen, and you're still you.

neighbors.heading: free in this very life
neighbors.text: Today Kabir spoke of jeevan mukat, freedom while still living. Buddhists know that shape. The Buddha described those who, in this very life, see clearly and let craving go out like a flame, then go on walking, eating and teaching. Buddhists call that going-out nirvana, and the one set free still breathes. The clench goes; the hand stays.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, freedom while living comes as the ego dissolves in remembering God, by the Guru's grace. For Buddhists, it comes by seeing through the sense of a lasting self until craving ends; the path doesn't rest on a Creator.
neighbors.shared: freedom can begin in the middle of an ordinary day.
neighbors.sources: Itivuttaka 44, the two kinds of nibbana (paraphrase) · Salok Kabir, Ang 1365 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: until you stand in their place
neighbors.text: Today Farid said: don't keep a book of other people's faults; bow your head and look within your own collar. Jewish sages say something close. Hillel taught, in Pirkei Avot: don't judge your fellow until you've come to stand in their place. Another teaching there asks a person to judge everyone on the side of merit, giving the benefit of the doubt.
neighbors.difference: Farid's picture is bowing inward, the posture of prayer, to see your own faults before God. The rabbis' sayings sit within the Torah's call to fair judgment between neighbors, asking for honest courts as well as generous hearts.
neighbors.shared: be slow with the red pen, and quick with mercy.
neighbors.sources: Pirkei Avot 2:4 (2:5 in some editions) and 1:6 (paraphrase) · Salok Sheikh Farid, Ang 1378 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: turn to yourself
neighbors.text: Today Farid told the clever to stop keeping a book of other people's faults and look under their own collar. The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote the same note to himself in his private journal. When someone's fault offends you, he said, turn at once to yourself and ask where you've done something like it. Then anger has less to hold on to.
neighbors.difference: Farid looks inward by bowing, an act of prayer before God, the Master in every heart. Marcus looked inward by reason, a Stoic exercise for keeping his own judgment clear and fair.
neighbors.shared: looking inward first makes us kinder to everyone else.
neighbors.sources: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 10.30 (paraphrase) · Salok Sheikh Farid, Ang 1378 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the devotion reaches Him
neighbors.text: Today young Namdev brought a cup of milk and trusted it would be received. The Qur'an speaks of offerings too, the animals offered and shared out as food at the pilgrimage, and says: "Their flesh and their food reach not Allah, but the devotion from you reacheth Him." What rises isn't the gift itself. It's the heart that brings it.
neighbors.difference: Namdev's hymn says the Lord smiled and drank, which some Sikhs read as a wonder and some as love closing the distance. In Islam, God has no need of food or drink at all; an offering's worth is the giver's devotion.
neighbors.shared: a small gift, given with your whole heart, is never small.

neighbors.heading: a leaf, a flower, a little water
neighbors.text: Today Namdev offered a cup of milk with a child's plain trust. Hindus hear Krishna in the Bhagavad Gita say something close: whoever offers him with love a leaf, a flower, a fruit or a little water, that offering of devotion he accepts. The size of the gift doesn't matter. The love in it does. Namdev's songs grew in that same world of bhakti.
neighbors.difference: For many Hindus, Krishna is God come in form, and offerings are often made before a sacred image. The Gurus taught that the One is formless and unborn, and asked Sikhs for love and the Name rather than offerings to an image.
neighbors.shared: what you bring matters less than how you bring it.

neighbors.heading: fragrance against the wind
neighbors.text: Today Ravidas sang that a castor plant beside sandalwood comes away fragrant. Buddhists reach for the same wood. The Dhammapada says the scent of flowers and sandalwood can't travel against the wind, "but the odour of good people travels even against the wind." And the Buddha told Ananda that good friendship isn't half the holy life. It's the whole of it.
neighbors.difference: For Ravidas, the fragrance is the Lord's own, settling into a lowly devotee, and the holy company is where it's met. For Buddhists, the fragrance is virtue a person grows by practice, helped by good friends, not a gift from a Creator.
neighbors.shared: who you stand beside slowly becomes part of who you are.
neighbors.sources: Dhammapada 54 (Max Müller 1881) · Samyutta Nikaya 45.2, Upaddha Sutta (paraphrase) · Asa, Ravidas, Ang 486 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a sweet savour
neighbors.text: Today Ravidas sang that nearness to the Lord made a poor castor plant fragrant. Christians speak of a fragrance passed on by nearness too. Paul writes that God "maketh manifest the savour of his knowledge by us in every place," and adds: "For we are unto God a sweet savour of Christ." Those who stay near Christ, in this picture, start to carry his scent.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, the fragrance is Christ's, God made flesh, and believers share it by grace through faith. For Sikhs, the Lord is formless and never born, and the fragrance settles in through the holy company and the Name.
neighbors.shared: love rubs off on whoever stays close to it.

neighbors.heading: if anything is sacred
neighbors.text: Today Pipa, a king, sang that the body itself is the temple, with the lamp and the offering inside. Walt Whitman, the American poet, said it his own way in I Sing the Body Electric: "If any thing is sacred the human body is sacred." He meant every body, the worker's and the old man's, not only the beautiful ones.
neighbors.difference: Pipa finds the Supreme within the body, and says the True Guru reveals it. Whitman praises the body as sacred in itself, a poet's wide-open faith in the ordinary, without one teacher or path.
neighbors.shared: the body you woke up in today deserves some reverence.
neighbors.sources: Walt Whitman, I Sing the Body Electric, Leaves of Grass · Dhanasri, Pipa, Ang 695 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the temple of the Holy Ghost
neighbors.text: Today Pipa sang that the body is the temple, and the sacred is met inside it. Catholics hear Saint Paul: "Or know you not, that your members are the temple of the Holy Ghost, who is in you, whom you have from God; and you are not your own?" So the Church teaches care for the body, tired or sick, young or old.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, God the Holy Spirit dwells in the baptized, and the body will rise again at the end. For Sikhs, the One's light is already within every body, and the True Guru shows the seeker what was there all along.
neighbors.shared: the place you meet the holy is closer than you think.

neighbors.heading: take refuge in Me alone
neighbors.text: Today Sadhna came with empty hands and asked only for grace. Hindus hear a promise near the end of the Bhagavad Gita. Krishna tells Arjuna: let go of every other duty and take refuge in me alone; I will free you from all wrongs, do not grieve. Some Hindu teachers call that surrender prapatti: trusting the Lord's grace instead of your own record.
neighbors.difference: For many Hindus, Krishna is God in human form, and refuge is taken in him. For Sikhs, the grace Sadhna begs for is nadar, the gracious glance of the formless Lord, met through the Guru's word.
neighbors.shared: you can ask for help without a list of reasons you deserve it.

neighbors.heading: not for our righteousness
neighbors.text: Today Sadhna pleaded with no good deeds to show, only need. Jews pray in that spirit too. Daniel prays that his people bring their pleas not because of their own righteousness but because of God's great compassion. The line lives on in the morning prayers: Master of all worlds, not on our merits do we lay our pleas before you, but on your great mercy.
neighbors.difference: In Jewish prayer, God's mercy meets a covenant people, with the Torah's commandments still to keep and cherish. Sadhna's plea is to the Lord's nadar, the gracious glance the Sikh Gurus teach no one can earn or force.
neighbors.shared: mercy finds us before we've earned it.
neighbors.sources: Daniel 9:18 (paraphrase) · the morning prayer Ribon kol ha-olamim (paraphrase) · Bilaval, Sadhna, Ang 858 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: feed my sheep
neighbors.text: Today the Guru forgave two proud minstrels, and their song went into the scripture. Christians know a story like it. Peter denied Jesus three times. After the resurrection, Jesus asks him three times, do you love me, and each time hands him work: "Feed my sheep." The one who failed was given his place back, and letters bearing his name are read in the Bible.
neighbors.difference: Peter's forgiveness comes from Jesus, whom Christians worship as the risen Son of God. Satta and Balvand were forgiven by Guru Arjan; Sikhs honor the Gurus as carrying the one light, and hold that God is never born.
neighbors.shared: a mistake doesn't have to be the last word on anyone.
neighbors.sources: John 21:15–17 (KJV) · Ramkali ki Var, Satta and Balvand, Ang 966–968 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: no blame on you this day
neighbors.text: Today the Guru forgave the minstrels who had boasted against him, and kept their song. Muslims remember forgiving days too. In the Qur'an, Joseph forgives the brothers who sold him: no blame on you this day, he says; may God forgive you. The early biographies say the Prophet Muhammad spoke those words again to the people of Mecca who had driven him out.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, the Prophet forgives as God's messenger, and all forgiveness is finally God's, the Most Merciful. In the Sikh story, forgiveness also meant the minstrels' own ballad was placed in the Guru Granth Sahib and sung.
neighbors.shared: forgiveness can open the door wider than before.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 12:92 (paraphrase) · Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah, the conquest of Mecca (paraphrase) · Ramkali ki Var, Satta and Balvand, Ang 966–968 (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Mata Khivi, named in the Granth

neighbors.heading: I was hungry
neighbors.text: Today Mata Khivi's kitchen was praised in the Granth, generous down to the ghee. Catholics hear Jesus say: "For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink." Feeding the hungry heads the Church's list of the corporal works of mercy. In that light, a kitchen becomes a place to meet Christ.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, the hungry stranger carries Christ himself, as Jesus says in that passage. For Sikhs, the langar serves everyone alike, sitting together in rows, as a sign that every person carries the same divine light.
neighbors.shared: a kitchen can be one of the holiest rooms in the house.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 25:35 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2447 (paraphrase) · Ramkali ki Var, Ang 967 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: giving food, giving life
neighbors.text: Today Mata Khivi was remembered for a generous kitchen, rich with ghee. Buddhists honor the giver of food too. The Buddha told a laywoman, Suppavasa, that whoever gives food gives four gifts: life, beauty, ease and strength, and shares in those gifts herself. In Theravada lands, monks still walk with bowls, and households practice dana, giving, by filling them.
neighbors.difference: For Buddhists, giving is a practice that loosens grasping and brings merit in this life and beyond. For Sikhs, langar is seva offered in God's name, with everyone fed alike, giver and guest at one level.
neighbors.shared: a full plate, handed over gladly, feeds two people.
neighbors.sources: Anguttara Nikaya 4.57, Suppavasa (paraphrase) · Ramkali ki Var, Ang 967 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the bandit who became a sage
neighbors.text: Today we met Bidhi Chand, a thief whose life turned when he came to the Guru. The Talmud tells of Resh Lakish, a bandit who saw Rabbi Yochanan bathing in the Jordan and leapt in after him. Yochanan told him: your strength belongs to Torah. Resh Lakish turned, studied, and became one of the great sages, Yochanan's own study partner.
