neighbors.difference: Bidhi Chand's change came through the Guru's company and the Name, and his old cunning was put to the Guru's service. For Jews, turning back is teshuvah, and Resh Lakish's new life was poured into Torah study.
neighbors.shared: your old strength can be turned to a new purpose.
neighbors.sources: Talmud Bava Metzia 84a (paraphrase) · Bhai Bidhi Chand and the horses, Sikh tradition (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: you belong to good now
neighbors.text: Today we met Bidhi Chand, who stole to live until a new company turned his life around. Victor Hugo told a story like that in Les Misérables. Jean Valjean, just out of prison, steals a bishop's silver. Caught and dragged back, he watches the bishop hand him the candlesticks too, and hears that he no longer belongs to evil, but to good.
neighbors.difference: Bidhi Chand's turning is told as Sikh tradition, made by the Guru's company and the Name. Valjean is a novelist's invention, and what changes him is one stranger's undeserved mercy.
neighbors.shared: someone believing in you can change the whole road.
neighbors.sources: Victor Hugo, Les Misérables, part 1, book 2 (paraphrase) · Bhai Bidhi Chand and the horses, Sikh tradition (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: with the steadfast
neighbors.text: Today Mata Nanaki waited through the Bakala years, holding on to a promise without pushing or complaining. Muslims call that kind of waiting sabr: patient, steady trust. The Qur'an says: "Seek help in steadfastness and prayer. Lo! Allah is with the steadfast." Sabr isn't doing nothing. It's staying faithful while the answer takes its time.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, sabr is a virtue the Qur'an praises in trouble and in obeying God, for every believer. Mata Nanaki's waiting, in the Sikh story, is tied to one promise: that her son would one day sit in the Guru's seat.
neighbors.shared: waiting with trust is its own kind of strength.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 2:153 (Pickthall 1930) · Mata Nanaki and the Bakala years, Sikh tradition (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: Shabari waits for Rama
neighbors.text: Today Mata Nanaki waited for years, sure a promise would keep itself. Hindus tell of Shabari, an old forest woman who waited her whole life for Rama to come. Each day, the tellings say, she gathered fruit for him. When Rama finally came, he sat in her hermitage and gladly took what she offered.
neighbors.difference: For many Hindus, Rama is God come to earth, and Shabari's waiting ends in meeting him face to face. Mata Nanaki waited for a promise about her son and the Guru's seat; Sikhs revere the Gurus as one light, not God in human form.
neighbors.shared: love that waits is still love, every single day.
neighbors.sources: Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda, Shabari (paraphrase) · Mata Nanaki and the Bakala years, Sikh tradition (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: whoever would tend me
neighbors.text: Today a cook carried warm milk to a grandmother and two boys in a cold tower. Buddhists keep a story of the Buddha finding a monk lying sick and soiled, left alone. The Buddha and Ananda washed him and laid him on a bed. Then the Buddha told the monks: whoever would tend me should tend the sick.
neighbors.difference: Moti Ram's kindness cost him his life, and Sikhs honor him as a martyr. In the Buddhist story, care for the sick becomes part of the community's own rule of life, compassion as daily practice.
neighbors.shared: a small warm act, done in the cold, is never small.
neighbors.sources: Vinaya, Mahavagga 8.26 (paraphrase) · Moti Ram Mehra at Sirhind, Sikh tradition (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: I was in prison
neighbors.text: Today a cook brought warm milk to prisoners in a cold tower, at great cost. Christians hear Jesus describe the last judgment: "I was in prison, and ye came unto me." The surprised ask when, and he answers: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me."
neighbors.difference: For Christians, serving the prisoner is serving Christ himself, who says so in that passage. For Sikhs, Moti Ram served the Guru's own family, and he is honored as a martyr who paid with his life.
neighbors.shared: no one held in the cold should be forgotten.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 25:36, 40 (KJV) · Moti Ram Mehra at Sirhind, Sikh tradition (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: Antigone's handful of dust
neighbors.text: Today Todar Mal paid an outrageous price so a grandmother and two children could be cremated with dignity. The Greek play Antigone turns on the same duty. A king forbids anyone to bury Antigone's brother. She does it anyway, scattering dust over him, and pays dearly. She says she answers to older, unwritten laws than any king's.
neighbors.difference: Todar Mal, remembered as a Hindu of Sirhind, did this for another faith's family. Antigone acts for her own brother, in a tragedy that asks what happens when a ruler's law and the duty to the dead collide.
neighbors.shared: the dead are owed dignity, whatever it costs us.
neighbors.sources: Sophocles, Antigone (paraphrase) · Diwan Todar Mal and the cremation ground at Sirhind, Sikh tradition (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: Tobias buries the dead
neighbors.text: Today, tradition says, Todar Mal covered the ground with gold so a grandmother and two boys could have their rites. Catholic Bibles keep the Book of Tobias, where Tobias, a captive in Nineveh, buries his people's dead in secret against the king's order, and once leaves his own dinner to do it. Burying the dead is one of the Church's corporal works of mercy.
neighbors.difference: Catholics pray for the dead and await the resurrection of the body. Sikhs cremate their dead with the Guru's hymns, and Todar Mal, remembered as a Hindu of Sirhind, made that possible for another faith's family.
neighbors.shared: caring for the dead is one last way of loving them.
neighbors.sources: Book of Tobias, chapters 1–2 (Douay-Rheims, paraphrase) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2447 (paraphrase) · Diwan Todar Mal, Sikh tradition (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: satsang
neighbors.text: Today we gathered everyone around the Gurus and heard Guru Nanak's answer: the true company is where the one Name is praised. Hindus use the same word, satsang, the company of the true. In the Ramcharitmanas, Tulsidas sings that without satsang there's no real discernment, and that good company is the root of joy and blessing.
neighbors.difference: For Tulsidas, satsang is the company of Rama's devotees, and grace comes through Rama. For Sikhs, the sat sangat gathers around the Guru Granth Sahib, where the formless One's Name is sung.
neighbors.shared: the people you gather with help shape who you become.
neighbors.sources: Tulsidas, Ramcharitmanas, Bal Kand (paraphrase) · Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 72 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: responsible for one another
neighbors.text: Today we saw that the Gurus' story was never ten men alone; it was a whole company. Jewish sages put it in one line: all Israel are responsible for one another. Even the Amidah, said quietly by each person, asks in the plural: heal us, forgive us, hear our voice. Nobody carries the covenant alone.
neighbors.difference: In the Talmud, the bond is the covenant of Israel, sharing responsibility under the Torah. For Sikhs, the true company is known by what it does: it gathers where the one Name is praised.
neighbors.shared: nobody's story is theirs alone; it belongs to the company.
neighbors.sources: Talmud Shevuot 39a (paraphrase) · the Amidah (paraphrase) · Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 72 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the lot fell
neighbors.text: Today two sides agreed, before the slips touched the water, to accept whichever one floated. Christians remember a choice made in a similar way. After Judas was gone, the apostles prayed, put two names forward, and cast lots: "and the lot fell upon Matthias; and he was numbered with the eleven apostles." They trusted God with a choice they couldn't make alone.
neighbors.difference: In Acts, the lots come with prayer, asking God to show whom he had chosen. In the Sikh story, the test was also a way to keep the peace: both sides agreed first, so the side that lost could accept it.
neighbors.shared: agreeing on how to decide can keep a family together.
neighbors.sources: Acts 1:23–26 (KJV) · the Bandai and Tat Khalsa at Amritsar, Sikh tradition (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the cloak and the stone
neighbors.text: Today a fair test settled a quarrel before it turned violent. Muslims tell how the young Muhammad, before he was called as Prophet, settled one too. Mecca's clans, rebuilding the Kaaba, nearly came to blows over who would set the Black Stone back in place. He laid it on a cloak, had a leader from each clan lift an edge, and set it in with his own hands.
neighbors.difference: Muslims remember the cloak as a sign of the trustworthy man God would call as His Prophet. The Sikh story trusts a test both sides agreed to first, kept by Bhai Mani Singh, and the Guru's greeting floated.
neighbors.shared: a fair way forward lets everyone keep their dignity.
neighbors.sources: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah, the rebuilding of the Kaaba (paraphrase) · the Bandai and Tat Khalsa at Amritsar, Sikh tradition (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: servant of the servants
neighbors.text: Today the Khalsa gave a title to the man fanning the sangat, and he kept up his old service. Catholics hear Jesus settle his disciples' argument about who was greatest: "for he that is the lesser among you all, he is the greater." Popes have long called themselves the servant of the servants of God, a title Gregory the Great made his own.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, the pope's authority comes from Christ through Peter, and service is how it should be carried. For Sikhs, honor belongs to the Khalsa as a whole; Kapur Singh had his robe touched to five Sikhs' feet before he wore it.
neighbors.shared: the humblest helper in the room may be the true leader.
neighbors.sources: Luke 9:46–48 (Douay-Rheims) · Gregory the Great, the title servus servorum Dei (paraphrase) · Kapur Singh and the nawabship, Sikh tradition (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the quieter road
neighbors.text: Today Kapur Singh accepted honor only after it touched five Sikhs' feet, and kept cleaning the stables. The Dhammapada warns against the opposite. It pictures a foolish monk who wants a big name, a front seat among the monks and charge of the monasteries, and says such wanting only makes desire and pride grow. The wise, it says, take another road.
neighbors.difference: For Kapur Singh, humility was seva, selfless service offered to the Guru and the Khalsa. In the Dhammapada, letting go of rank is part of letting go of craving itself, on the road to nirvana.
neighbors.shared: honor sits lightest on the one who doesn't reach for it.
neighbors.sources: Dhammapada 73–75 (paraphrase) · Kapur Singh and the nawabship, Sikh tradition (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: nor bear any grudge
neighbors.text: Today we watched a minister's grief grow into a war on a whole people, and heard the word nirvair: without hate. Jews keep a commandment that guards the same door: "Thou shalt not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself."
neighbors.difference: Nirvair opens Sikh scripture as a word about God, and the Gurus call people to share it. In the Torah, these are commandments within the covenant, with courts of justice set alongside them, so wrongs are answered without private revenge.
neighbors.shared: grief is love; it doesn't have to turn into hate.
neighbors.sources: Leviticus 19:18 (JPS 1917) · Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, nirvair (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: not to become like the wrongdoer
neighbors.text: Today we saw a man's sorrow turn into cruelty, and heard the Gurus' word nirvair, without hate. The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius, who knew war and loss, wrote a short line to himself: "The best way of avenging thyself is not to become like the wrong doer." Grief, for him, was human. Turning into what hurt you was the real defeat.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, being without hate reflects God, who is nirvair, and is learned through the Name. For Marcus, it was the Stoic work of reason, keeping his own mind just, whatever others did.
neighbors.shared: you can carry grief without handing on hate.
neighbors.sources: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 6.6 (Long 1862) · Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, nirvair (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: who teacheth by the pen
neighbors.text: Today Baba Deep Singh copied the Granth by hand, one careful letter at a time. Muslims honor that desk too. In verses Muslims hold were among the first revealed, God is the one "Who teacheth by the pen." Muslim scribes and calligraphers copied the Qur'an slowly and beautifully, treating each letter of God's word as worth their whole attention.
neighbors.difference: Muslims hold the Qur'an as God's own speech in Arabic, and copying it serves that recited word. Sikhs honor the Guru Granth Sahib as the living Guru, holding hymns the Gurus and the saints sang themselves.
neighbors.shared: slow, careful work can be a form of love.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 96:4 (Pickthall 1930) · Ang 16, Sri Rag, Guru Nanak (paraphrase) · Baba Deep Singh at Damdama Sahib, Sikh tradition (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: Ganesha takes dictation
neighbors.text: Today Baba Deep Singh sat at the scribe's desk at Damdama, where tradition says the Granth was written out as it was spoken. Hindus tell of a famous scribe too. In a well-loved telling, the sage Vyasa recites the Mahabharata and Ganesha writes it down, on one condition: the pen must never stop. Vyasa agrees, if Ganesha understands every verse before he writes it.
neighbors.difference: For many Hindus, Ganesha is a form of God, honored as the remover of obstacles and patron of learning. Sikh scribes like Baba Deep Singh were devoted people, serving the Guru's word with their own hands.
neighbors.shared: the people who copy the words keep them alive for us.
neighbors.sources: Mahabharata, Adi Parva 1 (Ganguli, paraphrase) · Baba Deep Singh at Damdama Sahib, Sikh tradition (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: thus have I heard
neighbors.text: Today we saw how the stories of the hard century came down: chroniclers, outside records and family memory. Buddhist scriptures are honest about their own road. Many suttas open: "Thus have I heard." Tradition says Ananda, the Buddha's companion, recited them after the Buddha died, and monks chanted them together long before anyone wrote them down.
neighbors.difference: For Buddhists, those recited words are scripture, the Buddha's teaching passed on. The stories of the Sikhs' eighteenth century are history and memory, weighed with care, while the Guru Granth Sahib is the Guru.
neighbors.shared: being honest about how we know is a kind of respect.
neighbors.sources: the opening of the suttas, evam me sutam (Rhys Davids) · Vinaya, Cullavagga 11, the First Council (paraphrase) · the sources for eighteenth-century Sikh history (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: that which I also received
neighbors.text: Today we met three roads of memory, and why this path says "tradition says." Christians know that handing-on. Paul writes to the church at Corinth: "For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received." Here he's passing on what others told him, and naming who saw what.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, what Paul handed on is the heart of the faith: Christ's death and rising. The Sikh chronicles of the eighteenth century are history, honored and weighed, while the Guru's hymns are scripture.
neighbors.shared: every story we love reached us through someone's hands.
neighbors.sources: 1 Corinthians 15:3–8 (KJV) · the sources for eighteenth-century Sikh history (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: with malice toward none
neighbors.text: Today the Ardas named martyrs, not enemies, and ended asking for the good of all. Abraham Lincoln, closing a war that had torn his country apart, chose the same shape. In his second inaugural address he said: "With malice toward none, with charity for all." He asked the nation to bind up its wounds and care for the widow and the orphan.
neighbors.difference: The Ardas is a prayer to God, said at the close of Sikh gatherings, asking sarbat da bhala, the good of all. Lincoln's words were a president's speech, a civic hope for a divided nation, full of the Bible's language.
neighbors.shared: remember the brave, and wish good to everyone.
neighbors.sources: Abraham Lincoln, Second Inaugural Address (1865) · the Ardas, the remembrance of martyrs and its closing line (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: lay not this sin
neighbors.text: Today the Ardas remembered those who stood, and didn't curse those who struck. Catholics remember martyrs that way too, beginning with Stephen. As the stones fell, he knelt and cried: "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge." At Mass, the Church still names martyrs in its prayers, asking their help, never asking for revenge.
neighbors.difference: Catholics honor martyrs as saints who share in Christ's own death and now pray for the living. Sikhs remember martyrs in the Ardas for their courage and faith, and close by asking for the good of all.
neighbors.shared: remember the brave without passing on the bitterness.
neighbors.sources: Acts 7:59 (Douay-Rheims; 7:60 in many Bibles) · the Roman Canon of the Mass (paraphrase) · the Ardas (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: heat and cold come and go
neighbors.text: Today hunted riders sang in camps with no lamps, and called it chardi kala, rising spirits. Hindus hear a steadying word in the Bhagavad Gita. On a battlefield, Krishna tells a shaken Arjuna that heat and cold, pleasure and pain, come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, he says.
neighbors.difference: In the Ardas, Sikhs ask that rising spirits come through the Name, as a gift. In the Gita, Krishna points Arjuna to the Self within, which hard times cannot touch, and to doing his duty unshaken.
neighbors.shared: a hard season can pass through you without breaking you.

neighbors.heading: joy cometh in the morning
neighbors.text: Today hunted riders sang in camps with no lamps, and called it chardi kala, rising spirits. Jews know that kind of night. A psalm says: "weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning." And Rabbi Nachman of Breslov taught that being joyful, always, is a great mitzvah, a holy duty, even when you have to work at it.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, rising spirits flow from remembering the Name, asked for in every Ardas. For Rabbi Nachman, joy is itself a commandment, worked at through prayer, song and even dance, and the psalm finds the morning in God's favor.
neighbors.shared: a heavy night doesn't get the last word.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 30:5 (KJV; 30:6 in Jewish Bibles) · Rabbi Nachman of Breslov, Likutei Moharan II:24 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the carpenter
neighbors.text: Today a craftsman's son led riders, and craftsmen kept his name with pride. Christians remember a carpenter too. When Jesus taught in his hometown, the neighbors asked: "Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?" Before he preached, he worked with his hands, like Joseph, the carpenter who raised him.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, the carpenter of Nazareth is the Son of God, and his ordinary work shows God sharing ordinary life. Jassa Singh is honored as a Sikh chief and builder, a servant of the Guru's house.
neighbors.shared: work with your hands is never beneath anyone.

neighbors.heading: from the work of his hands
neighbors.text: Today a craftsman's son led riders, and craftsmen kept his name with pride. Muslims honor the work of the hands too. The Prophet Muhammad said that no one eats better food than what they earn with their own hands, and that the prophet David ate from the work of his hands. The Qur'an tells of David shaping coats of mail.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, David is a prophet and king, and his handwork is part of a prophet's example. Jassa Singh is honored as a chief who built forts and towers for the Guru's house, and his name came to belong to craftsmen.
neighbors.shared: honest work with your hands carries its own dignity.
neighbors.sources: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Sales, the hadith of David's handiwork (paraphrase) · Qur'an 34:10–11 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: it seemed good to us
neighbors.text: Today the bands of the Khalsa met before the Guru Granth Sahib to decide together. Catholics remember an early meeting like it. In Jerusalem, the apostles and elders gathered over a hard question and sent out their answer with these words: "it hath seemed good to the Holy Ghost and to us." The Church still meets in councils on great matters.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, the bishops in council, with the pope, teach with the Church's authority, guided by the Holy Spirit. The Sarbat Khalsa was the gathered community itself, deciding a gurmata in the Guru's presence, with no single head.
neighbors.shared: big choices are best made together, before something larger than us.
neighbors.sources: Acts 15:28 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 884 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: meeting in harmony
neighbors.text: Today the bands of the Khalsa met twice a year to decide together before the Guru. The Buddha gave his monks a similar way to stay strong. Near the end of his life, he said that as long as they met often, met in harmony, and did their business in harmony, they would grow and not decline.
neighbors.difference: The Buddha's monks decide by the rules of the Vinaya, with the Dhamma as their guide. The Sarbat Khalsa met before the Guru Granth Sahib, and its decision counted as the Guru's own resolution.
neighbors.shared: a community stays whole by meeting, listening and agreeing.

neighbors.heading: a king who copies the law
neighbors.text: Today a Maharaja struck coins in the Gurus' names, not his own. The Torah gives a king a task that points past himself too. He must write out a copy of the law, keep it beside him and read it all his days, "that his heart be not lifted up above his brethren."
neighbors.difference: For Jews, the king stands under the Torah, the covenant given to the whole people. Ranjit Singh's kingdom named itself the Khalsa's and gave its victory to the Gurus, whose word Sikhs keep in the Guru Granth Sahib.
neighbors.shared: power sits best with those who know it isn't theirs.

neighbors.heading: don't become a caesar
neighbors.text: Today a Maharaja put the Gurus' names on his coins instead of his own. A Roman emperor wrote a warning to himself in his private notebook. Marcus Aurelius told himself to take care not to be turned into a Caesar, not to be dyed in the purple, and to stay simple, good, just and kind.
neighbors.difference: Marcus Aurelius was keeping himself honest through philosophy and his own reason. Ranjit Singh's kingdom pointed past the king to the Gurus and to God, who, Sikhs say, gives every victory.
neighbors.shared: the bigger the job, the smaller the ego should be.

neighbors.heading: east and west
neighbors.text: Today the Harmandir got its gold, but tradition loves an older detail: doors on every side, open to anyone from any direction. The Qur'an has a line that opens every direction too: "Unto Allah belong the East and the West, and whithersoever ye turn, there is Allah's Countenance."
neighbors.difference: Muslims still face one direction together in prayer, toward the Kaaba in Mecca, while knowing God is not held there. At the Harmandir, the doors open on all sides, and people walk in from wherever they arrive.
neighbors.shared: whichever way you come from, you are not far from God.

neighbors.heading: from every side
neighbors.text: Today the Harmandir got its gold, but tradition loves an older detail: doors on every side, open to anyone from any direction. Hindus have an old prayer facing every way at once. A hymn of the Rig Veda opens by asking that good and noble thoughts come to us from every side.
neighbors.difference: The Rig Veda's line is a prayer, asking that wisdom arrive from everywhere. At the Harmandir, a kindred openness is built into the walls: a door for every direction and every visitor.
neighbors.shared: good things can come from any direction.

neighbors.heading: an old rule
neighbors.text: Today a Maharaja who could have killed chose, again and again, not to, and Kabir sings that where there is forgiveness, there is the Lord. The Buddha taught something close in the Dhammapada: "hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule."
neighbors.difference: Kabir's line finds the Lord himself where forgiveness is. The Buddha speaks of an old law of how things work, without naming a creator: letting go of hatred frees the one who lets it go.
neighbors.shared: mercy ends what anger only keeps going.
neighbors.sources: Dhammapada 5 (Max Müller 1881) · Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: be ye merciful
neighbors.text: Today a Maharaja who could have killed chose, again and again, not to, and Kabir sings that where there is forgiveness, there is the Lord. Jesus taught: "Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful." And on the cross, Luke says, he prayed: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do."
neighbors.difference: For Christians, human mercy flows from God's mercy shown in Jesus, who forgave even from the cross. Kabir's hymn says the Lord is present wherever forgiveness is, and the Maharaja is remembered as a ruler, not a saint.
neighbors.shared: mercy matters most in hands that could do otherwise.
neighbors.sources: Luke 6:36; Luke 23:34 (KJV) · Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: love that tells the truth
neighbors.text: Today Sikhs remembered a kingdom with pride, and with honesty about what went wrong. The writer James Baldwin held his own country the same way. He wrote that he loved America more than any other country, and for exactly that reason insisted on the right to criticize her, always.
neighbors.difference: Baldwin spoke as a citizen and writer, from his own conscience. Sikhs hold their memory to Guru Nanak's standard: truth is higher than everything, and higher still is truthful living.
neighbors.shared: you can love something and still tell the truth about it.
neighbors.sources: James Baldwin, Notes of a Native Son (1955), "Autobiographical Notes" (paraphrase) · Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 62 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a day of pardon
neighbors.text: Today Sikhs remembered a kingdom with pride, and with honesty about what went wrong. Catholics have done this in public too. On the first Sunday of Lent in 2000, Pope John Paul II led a Day of Pardon in Rome, asking God's forgiveness for wrongs done by members of the Church through the centuries, while giving thanks for its saints.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, the Church itself is holy, and the pope asked pardon for the sins of its sons and daughters. Sikhs measure their kingdom against the Gurus' teaching, and Sikh writers name the failings of its rulers, court and army.
neighbors.shared: an honest memory holds the gold and the failings together.
neighbors.sources: Pope John Paul II, homily for the Day of Pardon, 12 March 2000 (paraphrase) · International Theological Commission, Memory and Reconciliation (1999) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a mother left behind
neighbors.text: Today a queen was taken from Lahore, asked for her son, and wasn't given him. Hindus know a mother's grief like that from the Ramayana. When Rama is sent into the forest because of a promise made at court, his mother Kaushalya begs to go with him, and is left behind in the palace, grieving.
neighbors.difference: Kaushalya's sorrow belongs to a sacred epic, where Rama's exile is dharma kept, and it ends in his return. Jind Kaur's loss comes from the histories, still argued over, of a kingdom lost through war and treaty.
neighbors.shared: a crown can be taken; a mother's love doesn't let go.

neighbors.heading: rachel weeping
neighbors.text: Today a queen was taken from Lahore, asked for her son, and wasn't given him. Jews hear a mother like that in the prophet Jeremiah: "Rahel weeping for her children refused to be comforted for her children, because they were not." Then comes the promise: "they shall come again from the land of the enemy."
neighbors.difference: In Jeremiah, Rachel weeps for a whole people in exile, and God answers with a promise of return. Jind Kaur grieved for one boy, and Sikh memory keeps her as a queen who would not bow quietly.
neighbors.shared: a mother's tears are remembered, not hidden away.

neighbors.heading: faith from a mother
neighbors.text: Today a mother found her grown son again and told him who he was. Christians know a faith handed on that way. Writing to young Timothy, Paul remembers "the unfeigned faith that is in thee, which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois, and thy mother Eunice," and that from a child he had known the holy scriptures.
neighbors.difference: For Paul, the faith Timothy received from his mother and grandmother was faith in Christ. Jind Kaur gave her son his father's story and the Sikh faith he had been raised away from.
neighbors.shared: the people who love us first often hand us who we are.

neighbors.heading: restored to his mother
neighbors.text: Today a mother found her grown son again after long years apart. The Qur'an tells of a mother who had to let her baby go: the mother of Moses set him on the river. Then God brought him back to her: "So We restored him to his mother that she might be comforted and not grieve."
neighbors.difference: In the Qur'an, the reunion keeps God's promise to Moses's mother, and the child grows up to be a prophet. Jind Kaur's meeting with her son is history, long delayed by officials, and came when he was already a man.
neighbors.shared: even long years apart can end in a mother's arms.

neighbors.heading: my father's house
neighbors.text: Today the gurdwaras had slipped into a few private hands, and Sikhs asked what was still theirs. Catholics remember Jesus in the temple, turning over the money-changers' tables: "make not the house of my Father a house of traffic." Church law holds that the Church's goods are kept for worship, for those who serve, and for the poor.
neighbors.difference: In the Catholic Church, bishops and priests administer the Church's goods as stewards, under Church law. Sikhs hold that a gurdwara belongs to the sangat, and reformers worked for the community itself to manage its shrines.
neighbors.shared: a house of prayer is held in trust, never owned.

neighbors.heading: the sangha of the four directions
neighbors.text: Today the gurdwaras had slipped into a few private hands. The Buddha's monks were taught to hold things the other way round. In the Vinaya, monastery land and buildings are given to the sangha of the four directions, present and to come, and some of them may never be divided up or handed to any single monk.
neighbors.difference: In the Vinaya, the property belongs to the whole order of monks and nuns, everywhere and in every age. A gurdwara belongs to the sangat, the gathered Sikh community, with no order of monks in charge.
neighbors.shared: shared things need care, and belong to everyone who comes.

neighbors.heading: no form in the fire
neighbors.text: Today a reformer turned people back to the formless One and took the images away. Jews know that turn well. Moses reminds the people of the mountain: "ye saw no manner of similitude on the day that the LORD spake unto you in Horeb out of the midst of the fire." So no image of God is made.
neighbors.difference: In the Torah, the ban on images is a commandment of the covenant with Israel. For Sikhs, the formless One is praised in the Gurus' hymns, and the Guru Granth Sahib sits at the center of worship.
neighbors.shared: God is bigger than anything we could carve.

neighbors.heading: simplify, simplify
neighbors.text: Today a reformer took away the extra objects, the extra fees and the extra noise, until what was meant was left. Henry David Thoreau went to a cabin by a pond to try the same with a life. "Our life is frittered away by detail," he wrote in Walden. "Simplify, simplify."
neighbors.difference: Thoreau cleared a life to see what mattered to him, by his own lights. Baba Dayal cleared away rites to return to the Gurus' teaching: the Name of the formless One, and weddings before the Guru Granth Sahib.
neighbors.shared: sometimes the way forward is taking things away.
neighbors.sources: Henry David Thoreau, Walden (1854), "Where I Lived, and What I Lived For"

neighbors.heading: learn it and teach it
neighbors.text: Today a teacher spent his life pointing young Sikhs toward their own language and scripture. Muslims prize that work too. The Prophet Muhammad said that the best of you are those who learn the Qur'an and teach it. Many children who don't speak Arabic still learn its letters, to read the Qur'an in its own words.
neighbors.difference: Muslims hold the Qur'an to be God's own speech, revealed in Arabic. Sikhs keep the Gurus' hymns in Gurmukhi, and a human teacher, Sikhs say, points toward the Guru but is never the Guru.
neighbors.shared: a good teacher hands you the key to your own book.
neighbors.sources: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Virtues of the Qur'an (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the teacher as a god
neighbors.text: Today a teacher spent his life pointing young Sikhs toward their own language and scripture. Hindus give teachers a high seat. At the end of their studies, the Taittiriya Upanishad tells students: never neglect study and teaching, and treat your mother, your father and your teacher as gods.
neighbors.difference: In Hindu traditions, a living guru can be honored as a doorway to the divine. For Sikhs, the line of human Gurus ended, the Guru lives in the Granth and the Khalsa, and a teacher only points the way.
neighbors.shared: the people who teach us deserve our deep thanks.

neighbors.heading: jerome asks for help
neighbors.text: Today a translator worked with Sikh scholars to carry the Gurus' hymns into English. Christians remember Jerome, who spent years in Bethlehem turning the Bible into Latin. He learned Hebrew from Jewish teachers, and in his prefaces he wrote of how hard the work was, and of the help he sought so the words would come across true.
neighbors.difference: Jerome translated from inside his own faith, for the Church, and his Latin Bible became its common text. Macauliffe came to the Gurus' hymns from outside Sikhi, and asked Sikhs to check that his English matched what they sang.
neighbors.shared: carrying holy words between languages takes humility and help.

neighbors.heading: a room full of translators
neighbors.text: Today a translator worked with Sikh scholars to carry the Gurus' hymns into English. Buddhists remember Kumarajiva, a monk brought to China who turned Indian sutras into Chinese. Accounts say he worked with large teams of monks: he read and explained, they discussed, polished and wrote, until the words read true in Chinese.
neighbors.difference: Kumarajiva was a Buddhist monk, translating his own teachings for new Buddhists. Macauliffe came to the Gurus' hymns from outside Sikhi, and asked Sikh scholars to check the work.
neighbors.shared: a sacred text travels best in many careful hands.
neighbors.sources: Huijiao, Biographies of Eminent Monks, life of Kumarajiva (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: two solitudes
neighbors.text: Today the law recognized the Sikh wedding, four rounds around the Guru Granth Sahib. The poet Rilke wrote to young friends about what love asks. He described love as two solitudes that protect, border and greet each other, and said that in a good marriage each appoints the other guardian of their solitude.
neighbors.difference: Rilke speaks of two people keeping room for each other's inner life. In the lavan, the couple walk together toward the Lord, and the soul is the bride: the marriage points beyond the two of them.
neighbors.shared: love makes room for the other person to grow.
neighbors.sources: Rainer Maria Rilke, Letters to a Young Poet, letter 7 (1904); letter to Emanuel von Bodman (1901) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a great sacrament
neighbors.text: Today the law recognized the Sikh wedding, whose hymns make the soul the bride and the Lord the beloved. Catholics also see marriage pointing beyond the couple. Paul writes of husband and wife becoming one flesh, then adds: "This is a great sacrament; but I speak in Christ and in the church."
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, marriage is a sacrament, in the Latin Church given by bride and groom to each other, a sign of Christ's love for the Church. In the lavan, each soul is a bride of the one Lord, and the couple walk that path together.
neighbors.shared: a marriage can be a road two people walk toward God.
neighbors.sources: Ephesians 5:31–32 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1623 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: humility first
neighbors.text: Today volunteers walked to a garden humbly, took the blows, and got up again without striking back. Hindus find a list of those strengths in the Bhagavad Gita. Krishna names what true knowledge looks like in a person: humility, no pretense, ahimsa or not harming, patience and uprightness.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, Krishna lists these virtues as signs of knowing the Self. At Guru ka Bagh, the volunteers acted on Guru Nanak's word that sweetness and humility are the essence of goodness, under a vow to stay peaceful.
neighbors.shared: humble isn't the same as bowed.
neighbors.sources: Bhagavad Gita 13.7, 13.8 in some editions (paraphrase) · Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: walk humbly
neighbors.text: Today volunteers walked to a garden humbly, with no weapon and no curse, and got up each time they were knocked down. The prophet Micah asks what God wants of a person, and answers: "to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God." The Torah calls Moses very meek, and he stood before Pharaoh.
neighbors.difference: Micah's words sum up what God asks of a whole people bound by covenant. The volunteers lived Guru Nanak's word that sweetness and humility are the essence of virtue, under a vow of peace for one campaign.
neighbors.shared: a humble person can still stand very tall.

neighbors.heading: i was in prison
neighbors.text: Today a town lay across the rails so hungry prisoners on a train could eat. Jesus tells of the end of time, when the King says: "I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat" and "I was in prison, and ye came unto me." Those who fed and visited never knew they were serving him.
neighbors.difference: In Jesus's story, the hungry and the prisoner stand in for Christ himself. Sikhs fed the prisoners as langar, Guru Nanak's way of honest work and giving with your own hand, open to anyone.
neighbors.shared: a hungry person in chains is still a guest at the table.

neighbors.heading: and the prisoner
neighbors.text: Today a town lay across the rails so hungry prisoners on a train could eat. The Qur'an praises people who do just that: they "feed with food the needy wretch, the orphan and the prisoner, for love of Him," and say they want no reward or thanks, only to please God.
neighbors.difference: In the Qur'an, feeding the prisoner is a mark of the righteous, done for God alone. At Panja Sahib it was langar, Guru Nanak's free kitchen, and two Sikhs gave their lives so the meal could reach the train.
neighbors.shared: a meal for a stranger can be an act of worship.

neighbors.heading: the little way
neighbors.text: Today the path reached a thousand days, built one quiet day at a time. Catholics love a saint of small things. Thérèse of Lisieux called it her little way: doing small, ordinary things with great love. Jesus says it in the Gospel: "He that is faithful in that which is least, is faithful also in that which is greater."
neighbors.difference: For Thérèse, each small act is an offering of love to God and trust in his mercy. Sikhs carry seva and chardi kala, rising spirits, as they remember the Name day by day.
neighbors.shared: small days, kept faithfully, add up to a life.
neighbors.sources: Luke 16:10 (Douay-Rheims) · Thérèse of Lisieux, Story of a Soul (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: drop by drop
neighbors.text: Today the path reached a thousand days, built one quiet day at a time. The Buddha said it with a water jar. In the Dhammapada: "Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled; the wise man becomes full of good, even if he gather it little by little."
neighbors.difference: In the Dhammapada, good gathered little by little shapes a mind on the road to freedom. Sikhs hope each day of seva and the Name keeps the heart rising, in chardi kala, by God's will.
neighbors.shared: nothing you do well today is too small to count.

neighbors.heading: a whole world
neighbors.text: Today a man with no money carried a boy nobody else would carry, for years. The rabbis teach why one life matters so much. The Mishnah says a single person was created first, to teach that whoever saves one life is counted as if they had saved a whole world.
neighbors.difference: The Mishnah draws its lesson from Adam, one person from whom all people come. Sikhs see Puran Singh's carrying as seva, which Guru Nanak says earns a place of honor in God's court.
neighbors.shared: one person cared for is a whole world held up.
neighbors.sources: Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 (paraphrase) · Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 26 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a child at the well
neighbors.text: Today a man with no money carried a boy nobody else would carry, for years. The Chinese thinker Mencius believed every person has a heart that can't bear to see others suffer. His proof: anyone who suddenly sees a child about to fall into a well feels alarm and pity, before any thought of reward or praise.
neighbors.difference: Mencius saw that feeling as the seed of goodness in human nature, which each of us must grow. Puran Singh's life is remembered as seva, service offered while remembering God, with no sign on the door.
neighbors.shared: the urge to help is older than any reason for it.

neighbors.heading: who makes it grow
neighbors.text: Today Punjab's fields fed a nation, at a cost to water and soil. The Qur'an asks a question to carry into every field: "Have ye seen that which ye cultivate? Is it ye who foster it, or are We the Fosterer?" And the Prophet Muhammad told a companion washing for prayer not to waste water, even at a flowing river.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, people are trustees on the earth, answerable to God for how they use it. Guru Nanak calls the earth the great mother and water the father, and uses farming as a picture of the inner life.
neighbors.shared: the harvest is a gift, and the land deserves care back.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 56:63–64 (Pickthall 1930) · Sunan Ibn Majah 425, on not wasting water in ablution (paraphrase; some scholars grade its chain weak)

neighbors.heading: earth is my mother
neighbors.text: Today Punjab's fields fed a nation, at a cost to water and soil, and Guru Nanak calls the earth the great mother. Hindus have an old hymn to the earth in the Atharva Veda. It says: the earth is my mother, and I am her child. And it asks that whatever we dig from her may quickly grow back.
neighbors.difference: The Atharva Veda praises Prithvi, the earth, as a goddess and asks her blessing. Guru Nanak calls the earth mother in hymns to the one Creator, honoring her as part of his creation.
neighbors.shared: we take from the earth; we owe her our care.
neighbors.sources: Atharva Veda 12.1.12, 12.1.35 (paraphrase) · Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 8 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a day without work
neighbors.text: Today Sikhs scrubbed steps and cleared silt with their own hands, as kar seva. Zen monasteries have a name for that kind of work: samu, work practice, sweeping, cooking and weeding with full attention. Chan tradition remembers the old teacher Baizhang, who kept working in the fields in old age and said: a day without work, a day without eating.
neighbors.difference: In Zen, work is practice, a way of being wholly present with each task. In kar seva, Namdev's line holds both together: hands doing the work, and the mind kept with the Pure One, the Lord.
neighbors.shared: ordinary chores can hold a whole heart.
neighbors.sources: the sayings of Baizhang, as remembered in Chan tradition (paraphrase) · Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1376, Namdev's words in the Saloks of Kabir (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: do it heartily
neighbors.text: Today Sikhs scrubbed steps and cleared silt with their own hands, keeping their minds with the Lord as they worked. Paul gave the early Christians the same pairing: "whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men." Brother Lawrence, a monastery cook, said he felt as close to God among his pots as at prayer.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, the work is offered to Christ, the Lord Paul means. In kar seva, the work belongs to the Guru's house and the sangat, and is offered without asking for credit.
neighbors.shared: even washing a floor can be done for God.
neighbors.sources: Colossians 3:23 (KJV) · Brother Lawrence, The Practice of the Presence of God (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: someone to eat with
neighbors.text: Today a kitchen came along to a highway camp and fed anyone who sat down. Long ago the philosopher Epicurus taught, as Seneca passed it on, that you should look for someone to eat and drink with before you look for something to eat: a meal alone, he said, is the life of a lion or a wolf.
neighbors.difference: Epicurus was thinking of friends at one table, for a good life. Langar feeds strangers as equals, sitting in rows on the same ground, as seva in the Guru's house.
neighbors.shared: a meal is better when no one eats alone.

neighbors.heading: the soup line
neighbors.text: Today a kitchen came along to a highway camp and fed anyone who sat down. Catholics count feeding the hungry among the works of mercy, from Jesus's words: "For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat." Dorothy Day's Catholic Worker houses opened their doors and kept soup lines going for whoever came.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, feeding the hungry is serving Christ himself, present in the poor. Langar is the Guru's free kitchen, where everyone, rich or poor, sits on the same ground and eats the same food.
neighbors.shared: anyone who is hungry is welcome at the table.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 25:35 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2447 (paraphrase) · Dorothy Day, The Long Loneliness (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: one family
neighbors.text: Today a border ran between Sikhs and the places of Guru Nanak, and Guru Arjan sang that there is one father, and we are all his children. Hindus have an old line about the same wide family. The Maha Upanishad says the narrow mind counts people as mine or other; to the large-hearted, the whole world is one family.
neighbors.difference: The Upanishad's line is about how wide a wise heart can grow. Guru Arjan's hymn names the bond itself: one Creator, father of all, so every person is a brother or sister.
neighbors.shared: a border can't decide whose family you are.
neighbors.sources: Maha Upanishad 6.71–72, vasudhaiva kutumbakam (paraphrase) · Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 611 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: one father
neighbors.text: Today a border ran between Sikhs and the places of Guru Nanak, and Guru Arjan sang that there is one father, and we are all his children. The prophet Malachi asks it as a question: "Have we not all one father? hath not one God created us? why do we deal treacherously every man against his brother?"
neighbors.difference: Malachi speaks first to his own people, calling them back to the covenant God made with their ancestors. Guru Arjan's hymn reaches out to everyone at once, all children of the one father.
neighbors.shared: whoever is across the line is still a brother or sister.

neighbors.heading: to dress it and to keep it
neighbors.text: Today Sikh groups planted small, thick forests in honor of Guru Nanak. Christians read the job of tending the earth in the Bible's first pages: "the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it." Francis of Assisi praised God for Brother Sun, Sister Water and Mother Earth.
neighbors.difference: In Genesis, people are placed in the garden as its keepers, answerable to God. Guru Nanak's salok names air the Guru, water the father and the earth the great mother: family, as well as a trust.
neighbors.shared: planting a tree is a way of saying thank you.
neighbors.sources: Genesis 2:15 (KJV) · Francis of Assisi, Canticle of the Creatures (paraphrase) · Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 8 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a tree as charity
neighbors.text: Today Sikh groups planted small, thick forests in honor of Guru Nanak. The Prophet Muhammad praised that work. He said that when a Muslim plants a tree, whatever a bird, a person or an animal eats from it counts as charity for the one who planted it. Another saying tells you to plant your sapling even if the Hour has come.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, a tree's shade and fruit count as charity before God, and people are trustees of the earth. Guru Nanak names the earth the great mother, and the forests honor him with a gift back to her.
neighbors.shared: the shade you plant will cool someone you'll never meet.
neighbors.sources: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Agriculture, the hadith of planting (paraphrase) · Musnad Ahmad, the hadith of the sapling (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: names at the altar
neighbors.text: Today the Ardas carried the martyrs' memory, standing, and ended by asking good for all. Catholics say martyrs' names at prayer too. The Roman Canon, a prayer of the Mass, names women and men who gave their lives, Perpetua and Felicity, Agnes and Cecilia among them, and asks for a share in their company.
neighbors.difference: Catholics honor the martyrs as saints in heaven and ask them to pray for us. In the Ardas, Sikhs recall the martyrs to keep their courage close, and address their prayer to God alone.
neighbors.shared: the people who held on before us are not forgotten.

neighbors.heading: may all beings be well
neighbors.text: Today the Ardas remembered every loss and still ended with sarbat da bhala, the good of all. Buddhists chant a wish just as wide. In the Metta Sutta, the Buddha teaches a love that wishes: may all beings be happy and at ease, seen and unseen, near and far, born and yet to be born.
neighbors.difference: The Metta Sutta is a practice of the heart, growing goodwill like a mother's for her only child. The Ardas asks it of God: by your will, the good of all, through the Name.
neighbors.shared: after every loss, still wish good for everyone.

neighbors.heading: sitting on the floor
neighbors.text: Today some Sikh families slept on the floor to keep company with a grandmother and two boys in a cold tower. Jews know that kind of remembering. On Tisha B'Av, the day of mourning for the Temples, the custom is to sit on the floor or low stools and read Lamentations: "How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people!"
neighbors.difference: Tisha B'Av mourns a city and a Temple, the loss of a whole people's center, with a full fast. The Sahibzade week remembers four sons and their grandmother, and sleeping on the floor is a family custom, not a rule.
neighbors.shared: sometimes we give up comfort so memory has room.

neighbors.heading: grief needs a shape
neighbors.text: Today some Sikh families slept on the floor for a few nights so a hard memory would have room. Psychologists have found something like it. In studies by Michael Norton and Francesca Gino, people who had lost someone and kept a small ritual, a set act they repeated, reported less grief and felt more in control.
neighbors.difference: The research looks at rituals people make for themselves, of any kind, and measures how they feel. The Sahibzade week is a shared memory of martyrs, kept so their faith is honored, not only the sorrow.
neighbors.shared: grief carried in a ritual is easier to carry.
neighbors.sources: Michael Norton and Francesca Gino, "Rituals Alleviate Grieving for Loved Ones, Lovers, and Lotteries," Journal of Experimental Psychology: General (2014) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: servant of the merciful
neighbors.text: Today the hard century began with a man who called himself the Guru's banda, his servant. Muslims carry that word in their names: Abdullah, servant of God; Abd al-Rahman, servant of the Merciful. The Qur'an says those servants "walk upon the earth modestly, and when the foolish ones address them answer: Peace."
neighbors.difference: In Islam, a person is a servant of God alone, and no human being takes that place. Banda gave himself as the Guru's servant, and Sikhs hold that the Gurus carried the one God's light and word.
neighbors.shared: the proudest title can be servant.

neighbors.heading: dasa, the servant
neighbors.text: Today the hard century began with an ascetic who called himself the Guru's banda, his servant. Hindus love that title too. In the Ramayana, Hanuman, strong enough to leap the sea, introduces himself simply as Rama's servant. Hindu names like Ramdas and Haridas carry the same word: servant of God.
neighbors.difference: For Hanuman, serving Rama is serving God in a form he loves. Banda served Guru Gobind Singh, and Sikhs honor the Gurus as carrying the one God's light, not as God in a body.
neighbors.shared: the strongest can choose to serve.

neighbors.heading: one mouthful
neighbors.text: Today a hymn walked a whole life through four watches of the night, and asked which watch it is now. Buddhists ask that too. The Buddha once asked his monks how often they thought of death. One said, for a day; another, for a meal. He praised the two who said: for one mouthful, and for one breath in and out.
neighbors.difference: In the hymn, the merchant friend is called back to the Name before the night ends. Buddhists don't turn to a God here; remembering death spurs practice, letting go of clinging while there is time.
neighbors.shared: this hour is the one we're given.

neighbors.heading: number our days
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak sang a life in four watches of the night, and asked which watch it is now. Christians pray that question too. A psalm asks God: "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom." And Jesus told of a rich man building bigger barns, who didn't know his life would be asked of him that night.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs answer the passing night with remembrance of the Name. Christians number their days in hope of resurrection and life with God through Christ.
neighbors.shared: a short life is a reason to wake up, not to fear.

neighbors.heading: seeing the better
neighbors.text: Today a Guru admitted the mind won't do what it's told, and kept going, gently. People on their own path know that sentence. The Roman poet Ovid gave Medea a line still quoted: I see the better way and approve it, and I follow the worse. One study found that meeting a slip with kindness, not scolding, helped people try again.
neighbors.difference: In the hymn, the stubborn mind is turned by remembering the Name each day. Ovid and the study offer no God; the turning comes from honest self-knowledge, patience and practice.
neighbors.shared: slipping back isn't the end; you begin again, gently.
neighbors.sources: Ovid, Metamorphoses 7.20–21 (paraphrase) · Breines and Chen, "Self-Compassion Increases Self-Improvement Motivation" (2012) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the good which i will
neighbors.text: Today a Guru said the mind won't listen, however often it's taught. Catholics hear Saint Paul say the same: "For the good which I will, I do not; but the evil which I will not, that I do." Paul doesn't end in despair; he ends in thanks for grace. Catholics bring that same struggle to confession, again and again.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the stubborn mind is steadied by remembering the Name. For Catholics, the struggle is a wound left by original sin, healed by Christ's grace, especially in the sacraments.
neighbors.shared: an honest "i keep slipping" is already a kind of prayer.

neighbors.heading: by that light
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak made the sky an aarti tray, with the sun and moon for lamps. Hindus, who wave the lamp at home and in temple, know that turn too. An Upanishad says the sun does not shine there, nor the moon and stars; when the One shines, everything shines after, and all this is lit by that light.
neighbors.difference: For many Hindus, the lamp waved before a sacred image is a loving offering in itself. Guru Nanak's hymn sets the tray aside: the whole universe is already performing the aarti.
neighbors.shared: every light you see can turn your heart to its source.

neighbors.heading: the heavens declare
neighbors.text: Today the whole sky became an aarti: sun and moon the lamps, stars the pearls. Jews sing a sky like that. A psalm says: "The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament showeth His handiwork." Another calls on creation itself: "Praise ye Him, sun and moon; praise Him, all ye stars of light."
neighbors.difference: In the Sikh hymn, the sky is already worshiping, so no lamp needs lighting. In Judaism, the heavens' praise sits beside commanded acts, like Shabbat candles lit by hand for the God of Israel.
neighbors.shared: look up tonight; the sky is already praising.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 19:2 and Psalm 148:3 (JPS 1917; Psalm 19:1 in many Bibles)

neighbors.heading: without me
neighbors.text: Today a morning hymn began with plain need: without the Lord, my mind cannot live. Christians hear Jesus say it from the other side: "I am the vine, ye are the branches... for without me ye can do nothing." And the first blessing in his Sermon on the Mount goes to need: "Blessed are the poor in spirit."
neighbors.difference: In the hymn, the Guru brings the seeker to meet the Lord, the breath of life. For Christians, Jesus himself is the vine, God made flesh, and the branches live by staying in him.
neighbors.shared: admitting you need help is where strength begins.

neighbors.heading: ye are the poor
neighbors.text: Today a morning raga opened by admitting need, no armor on yet. Muslims start the day the same way, rising before the sun for the dawn prayer, Fajr. The Qur'an names the need plainly: "O mankind! Ye are the poor in your relation to Allah. And Allah! He is the Absolute, the Owner of Praise."
neighbors.difference: In the hymn, the Lord is the beloved breath, met through the Guru. Muslims turn to Allah directly in set prayers five times a day, and Allah, who needs nothing, is never described as needing us back.
neighbors.shared: admitting you need help is where strength begins.

neighbors.heading: a clean heart
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak washed the pot before the milk went in. Catholics pray for a clean vessel too. A psalm asks: "Create a clean heart in me, O God: and renew a right spirit within my bowels." Before Communion, Catholics examine their conscience, and confess serious sin first, readying the vessel to receive.
neighbors.difference: In the hymn, the cleaning is a daily discipline of good deeds and the Name. Catholics believe the heart is made clean by God's grace in confession, and what they receive is Christ himself.
neighbors.shared: wash the pot first; something good is on its way.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 50:12 (Douay-Rheims; Psalm 51:10 in many Bibles) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1385 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: purify the mind
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak washed the pot first, then brought the milk, and churned with patience. Buddhists start there too. A verse of the Dhammapada sums up the whole teaching: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened."
neighbors.difference: In the hymn, the clean vessel is made ready for the one Name and union with the Lord. Buddhists purify the mind by their own practice, to be free of craving, not to meet a creator God.
neighbors.shared: make room inside before you ask for something new.

neighbors.heading: a weaned child
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak stepped out of the lineup of the learned: I know nothing; I know only your Name. Jews sing a psalm of the same calm: "neither do I exercise myself in things too great, or in things too wonderful for me. Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul; like a weaned child with his mother."
neighbors.difference: Guru Nanak rests in the one Name through the Guru's Word. Jews sing this psalm before the God of Israel, and still prize hard study of Torah; there, humility and learning walk together.
neighbors.shared: saying "i don't know" can be the calmest sentence of the day.

neighbors.heading: i neither know
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak didn't compete with the scholars; he said, I know nothing. People on their own path honor that move. In Plato's Apology, Socrates questions a man famed for wisdom and walks away thinking: "I neither know nor think that I know." For Socrates, that honest not-knowing was where wisdom starts.
neighbors.difference: Guru Nanak's not-knowing rests in the one Name and asks the Lord's kindness. Socrates' not-knowing keeps him asking questions; it leans on reason and examination rather than devotion.
neighbors.shared: saying "i don't know" can be the calmest sentence of the day.

neighbors.heading: the devotion reacheth him
neighbors.text: Today Namdev brought a cup of milk, and what reached the Lord was his heart. Muslims hear the same at Eid al-Adha. The Qur'an says of the sacrifice: "Their flesh and their blood reach not Allah, but the devotion from you reacheth Him." The meat is shared with family, neighbors and the poor.
neighbors.difference: In Namdev's hymn, the Lord smiles and drinks the milk. Muslims hold that Allah needs nothing and takes no food; the offering feeds people, and the devotion is what rises to Him.
neighbors.shared: what reaches heaven is the heart you carry it in.

neighbors.heading: a leaf, a flower
neighbors.text: Today Namdev carried a cup of milk and begged the Lord to drink. Hindus know that cup; Namdev is still sung as a saint in Maharashtra's Varkari tradition. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says that a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, offered with devotion, he accepts, given in love.
neighbors.difference: Many Hindus offer food before a sacred image, then share it as prasad, a blessing. Sikhs read Namdev's cup, placed in the Granth, as devotion to the One beyond form, met without images.
neighbors.shared: what reaches heaven is the heart you carry it in.
neighbors.sources: Bhagavad Gita 9.26 (paraphrase) · Namdev in the Varkari tradition (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: one great cloud
neighbors.text: Today rain fell on every field, and a leather worker's son was honored. Buddhists tell a rain story too: in the Lotus Sutra, one great cloud rains on every plant alike, and each grows in its own way. And in an older sutta, the Buddha says no one is low or noble by birth, only by deeds.
neighbors.difference: Ravidas is lifted by the Lord's Name, a grace from beyond him. For Buddhists, the rain is the Buddha's teaching, and freedom comes by walking the path oneself, without a creator God.
neighbors.shared: the rain falls on every field alike.
neighbors.sources: Lotus Sutra, chapter 5, the parable of the plants (paraphrase) · Vasala Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.7 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: rain on the just
neighbors.text: Today the rain fell on every field, and a leather worker's son was honored for the Name. Jesus pointed at the same sky: God "maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust." And Peter, in a Roman officer's home, said: "God is no respecter of persons."
neighbors.difference: Ravidas is honored through the Name, his hymns sung beside the Gurus' own. Christians speak of grace given in Christ, gathering a church where birth and rank don't decide your seat.
neighbors.shared: grace doesn't check your family name first.

neighbors.heading: nothing human is foreign
neighbors.text: Today a Guru said: no one is my enemy, no one is a stranger. People on their own path reach for an old line. The Roman playwright Terence gave a character the words still quoted: I am human, so nothing human is foreign to me. Philosophers since have taken it as a whole way of meeting people.
neighbors.difference: In the hymn, strangers vanish because the One is present in everyone, seen in holy company. Terence's line asks for no belief in God; it rests on shared humanity alone.
neighbors.shared: the person at the next table is not a stranger.

neighbors.heading: who is my neighbour
neighbors.text: Today a Guru said: no one is my enemy, no one a stranger. Catholics hear Jesus push the same way: "Love your enemies: do good to them that hate you." And when a lawyer asked, "who is my neighbour?", Jesus told of a Samaritan, a foreigner, who stopped for a wounded man on the road.
neighbors.difference: In the hymn, jealousy falls away in holy company and the One is seen in all. Catholics love even enemies because Christ commanded it, seeing each person as made in God's image, and lean on grace to do it.
neighbors.shared: no one is a stranger once you've really seen them.

neighbors.heading: a lotus leaf
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak pointed to a lotus and a duck: in the water all day, never soaked. Hindus know the lotus picture well. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says one who acts without clinging, offering every act to the divine, is untouched, like a lotus leaf by water. And he told Arjuna to stay and act, not run away.
neighbors.difference: Many Hindus also honor the renouncer, the sannyasi, as a holy path and stage of life. Guru Nanak pointed the yogis back to the household as the place to live untouched.
neighbors.shared: you can be in the water and still stay dry.

neighbors.heading: torah and a trade
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak told the yogis you don't have to leave the stream to stay dry. Jewish teaching also keeps holiness inside ordinary life. In Pirkei Avot, a sage says Torah study is best joined with a worldly trade, because the effort of both keeps wrongdoing out of mind. A home, a table, a job: there the commandments are kept.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, staying untouched comes from keeping the One Name settled in the mind. For Jews, it comes through living Torah's commandments, given to Israel, in every part of the day.
neighbors.shared: holiness can live at a kitchen table, not only a mountaintop.

neighbors.heading: put on kindness
neighbors.text: Today the yogis offered Nanak their earrings and coat, and he chose to wear the Word inside. Christians are told to dress the same way: "Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering." An older verse says: "man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart."
neighbors.difference: Many Sikhs keep outward articles too, like the turban and the Five Ks, with the Word within. For Christians, the deepest clothing is Christ himself: "put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ."
neighbors.shared: what you wear inside is the part people feel.

neighbors.heading: the raiment of restraint
neighbors.text: Today Nanak traded the yogis' earrings for the Word worn within. The Qur'an speaks of clothing the same way: "We have revealed unto you raiment to conceal your shame, and splendid vesture, but the raiment of restraint from evil, that is best." A hadith adds that Allah looks not at your bodies or faces, but at your hearts.
neighbors.difference: Muslims keep outward signs too, like modest dress and the set movements of prayer, as obedience to Allah's revealed law. Many Sikhs wear the Five Ks, and Nanak taught the Word as the earring no one sees.
neighbors.shared: the best clothes are the ones nobody sees.

neighbors.heading: with modesty
neighbors.text: Today Nanak answered the yogis' hard questions without mocking them. Catholics are asked to answer that way: "being ready always to satisfy every one that asketh you a reason of that hope which is in you. But with modesty and fear." The Church also teaches that it rejects nothing true and holy in other religions.
neighbors.difference: Nanak answered from the Word, turning the yogis' own terms toward the Name. Catholics enter dialogue honoring what is true in others, while proclaiming Christ as the way, the truth and the life.
neighbors.shared: you can disagree and still leave the other person heard.

neighbors.heading: well-spoken words
neighbors.text: Today Nanak met pointed questions with patient answers, never mockery. Buddhists call that skill right speech. The Buddha said well-spoken words have five marks: spoken at the right time, true, gentle, helpful, and said with goodwill. He too often met other teachers in conversation, taking up their words and giving them new meaning.
neighbors.difference: Nanak turned the yogis' words toward the one Name and the Guru's Word. The Buddha turned old words, like brahmin or the sacred fire, toward his path of awakening, without a creator God.
neighbors.shared: a kind answer can carry a hard truth.

neighbors.heading: study and doing
neighbors.text: Today the pandit read and argued, but had he understood? Jews prize study deeply, and still ask that question. In Pirkei Avot, a sage says: not study but doing is the main thing. And when the rabbis debated which is greater, study or deeds, they answered study, because it leads to doing.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the treasure is the Name within, which reading alone can miss. In Judaism, Torah study is itself a commandment and a form of worship, and it bears fruit in keeping the commandments.
neighbors.shared: the best reading is the one that changes how you live.

neighbors.heading: for life, not for school
neighbors.text: Today the pandit could quote every page and still miss the treasure inside him. People on their own path have said this a long time. Seneca complained that we learn for the classroom, not for life. And Montaigne wrote that we labor to stuff the memory, and leave understanding and conscience empty.
neighbors.difference: Guru Nanak points the reader to the Name, the treasure within. Seneca and Montaigne point to wisdom lived out, a good life built on reason and character, which needs no belief in God.
neighbors.shared: a full shelf isn't the same as a changed heart.
neighbors.sources: Seneca, Moral Letters 106 (paraphrase) · Montaigne, Essays I.25, "Of Pedantry" (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: what he did with it
neighbors.text: Today the Patti said you're truly read only when you can give an account of your life. Muslims hear the same test. A hadith says that on the Last Day each person is asked about their life, how they spent it, and about their knowledge, what they did with it. The Prophet prayed for refuge from knowledge that does not benefit.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, learning shows in seeing the One in all and letting go of "I, I." For Muslims, beneficial knowledge is lived in obedience to Allah, and the account is given on a Day of Judgment.
neighbors.shared: what you know is measured by what you do with it.

neighbors.heading: the higher knowledge
neighbors.text: Today the Patti said reading isn't the finish line. Hindus have a famous version. In the Mundaka Upanishad, a teacher says there are two kinds of knowledge. The lower is the Vedas themselves, with grammar and the other learned arts. The higher is the knowledge by which the Imperishable is known.
neighbors.difference: In the Upanishad, the higher knowledge comes through a teacher and meditation on Brahman, the Imperishable. In the Patti, it comes through the Guru's Word and the Name, and shows in a humble life.
neighbors.shared: the letters are a door; living them is walking through.

neighbors.heading: the world is burning
neighbors.text: Today the summer burned, and the bride felt the heat of being apart. Buddhists name that heat honestly. In his first teaching, the Buddha said being separated from what we love is suffering. He also spoke of the whole world burning, with craving, aversion and confusion, and of the freedom that comes when that fire goes out.
neighbors.difference: In the Barah Maha, the cure for the heat is nearness to the Beloved, God. For Buddhists, the cooling comes from letting go of craving itself, not from meeting a God.
neighbors.shared: it's honest to say it: being apart hurts.
neighbors.sources: Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 56.11 (paraphrase) · Adittapariyaya Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 35.28 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a dry and thirsty land
neighbors.text: Today the earth burned, and the bride, apart from her Beloved, prayed and looked for shade. Christians pray from that same heat. A psalm says: "my soul thirsteth for thee, my flesh longeth for thee in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is." Another calls the LORD "thy shade upon thy right hand."
neighbors.difference: In the Barah Maha, the longing is a bride's for the Beloved, met through the Name. Christians pray these psalms as longing for God, answered in Christ, who promised "living water."
neighbors.shared: the thirst itself can be a kind of prayer.

neighbors.heading: love made visible
neighbors.text: Today the story of Lalo's plain bread made honest work part of the path. People on their own path say this too. In The Prophet, Kahlil Gibran writes: "Work is love made visible." And: "if you bake bread with indifference, you bake a bitter bread that feeds but half man's hunger."
neighbors.difference: Guru Nanak ties honest work to remembering the Name and giving from your hand. Gibran's prophet speaks of love and life, not a set path or God's command; readers take him as they choose.
neighbors.shared: what you make with care feeds more than hunger.

neighbors.heading: working with his hands
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak said the one who earns by effort and gives from his hand knows the path. Catholics read almost the same: "let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have something to give to him that suffereth need." Saint Benedict's Rule calls idleness the enemy of the soul.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, honest work stands beside remembering the Name and sharing. For Catholics, work shares in God's creating and in Christ's own years as a carpenter, offered up to God.
neighbors.shared: honest hands and an open hand belong together.
neighbors.sources: Ephesians 4:28 (Douay-Rheims) · Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 48 (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: You are the form of light

neighbors.heading: know the self
neighbors.text: Today a Guru told the mind: you are the form of light; know your origin. Hindus know that call. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says the living self in every being is an eternal part of him. And in an Upanishad, a sage tells his wife that when the true Self is seen and known, all this is known.
neighbors.difference: Hindu schools differ: some hold the true Self is one with Brahman, others that the soul stays forever distinct, serving God. The Guru says you are light, so seek the Lord who is its source.
neighbors.shared: underneath the noise, there is light in you.

neighbors.heading: the lamp of the lord
neighbors.text: Today a Guru told the mind it is a form of light, and to know where it came from. Jews have a lamp verse too: "The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD." And Genesis tells how God breathed the breath of life into the first human, made in God's own image.
neighbors.difference: The Guru speaks of the mind as light from the One, seeking its source. In Judaism, the soul is God's lamp, a gift from its Maker, and its light is lived by keeping Torah's commandments.
neighbors.shared: you carry a light you didn't make, and you can tend it.

neighbors.heading: restless until
neighbors.text: Today a Guru told the restless mind: no one has found Him through cleverness. Paul wrote something close: "the world by wisdom knew not God." And Augustine prayed: "Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee."
neighbors.difference: In the Anand, rest comes through the True Guru and the Word, sung. For Christians, rest comes through Jesus, who said: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."
neighbors.shared: a restless heart is looking for home, not a better argument.

neighbors.heading: hearts find rest
neighbors.text: Today Guru Amar Das told the restless mind that cleverness won't bring it home; rest comes through the Word. Muslims know that rest too. The Qur'an says: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!" That remembrance, dhikr, is often a few sacred words repeated on prayer beads, again and again.
neighbors.difference: In the Anand, rest comes through the Guru's Word, sung in the sangat. For Muslims, dhikr remembers Allah in words from the Qur'an and the Prophet's practice.
neighbors.shared: a tired mind can rest in a word repeated with love.

neighbors.heading: pray without ceasing
neighbors.text: Today the remembering went on past the morning, sitting and standing, with every breath and bite. Catholics know that thread. Saint Paul wrote: "Pray without ceasing." Brother Lawrence, a Carmelite who worked in a monastery kitchen, said the clatter of pots didn't break his prayer; he kept God company at work as on his knees.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the thread is the Name, remembered through the Guru's Word. For Catholics, it is friendship with God in Christ, fed by the Mass and the Church's set prayers through the day.
neighbors.shared: prayer can ride along with the dishes.
neighbors.sources: 1 Thessalonians 5:17 (Douay-Rheims) · Brother Lawrence, The Practice of the Presence of God (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: walking, standing, sitting
neighbors.text: Today the remembering went on all day, sitting and standing, with every breath and mouthful. Buddhists practice something close. In a core teaching on mindfulness, the Buddha says to know it when walking, standing, sitting or lying down, and to be fully aware while eating and drinking. The breath is a place to come back to.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs remember the Name of the One through the day. Buddhist mindfulness attends to body, feelings and mind just as they are, as a path to freedom, not as remembrance of a God.
neighbors.shared: every breath and every bite is a chance to come back.

neighbors.heading: days as grass
neighbors.text: Today Guru Arjan asked, again and again, where is mother, where is father, and named what stays: remembrance of the Lord. A psalm walks the same line: "As for man, his days are as grass... For the wind passeth over it, and it is gone." Then it turns: "But the mercy of the LORD is from everlasting to everlasting."
neighbors.difference: Sikhs meet passing with remembrance of the Name. Jews meet it with trust in God's lasting covenant love, and by remembering their dead, saying Kaddish and honoring parents as a commandment.
neighbors.shared: love your people fully; let something deeper hold the weight.

neighbors.heading: given back
neighbors.text: Today a verse asked where mother, father and children go, and named what doesn't pass. People on their own path ask too.
